meta.blurb: In 1910 a writer claimed that getting rich follows laws, like arithmetic. Some of Wallace Wattles's advice is sensible, and some is pure belief. This retelling keeps his boldest ideas and tells you honestly which is which.
meta.bible: Wallace D. Wattles: an American writer; he published The Science of Getting Rich in 1910 and died in 1911. He also wrote The Science of Being Well and The Science of Being Great. The book has a short preface and 17 chapters. Thinking Substance: Wattles's name for the one living material that he believed fills the universe and makes all things; this is his belief and is not proven science. Gratitude: thankfulness, which Wattles says keeps the mind close to what is good. Increase: his word for growth in life and wealth. Use Value and Cash Value: his terms for what a thing is worth in use and what it costs in money. The Certain Way: his phrase for his method. The competitive plane and the creative plane: his two ways of living and working. The Advancing Man: his name for an employee who grows. Thinkers he names as earlier sources of his main idea: Spinoza, Hegel and Emerson. Thomas Edison: an American inventor, used once as an example of patient trying. Voice and tone: warm, clear, honest and encouraging; Wattles's claims are always given as his own beliefs, never as proven facts; modern cautions are noted gently; no invented quotes, numbers or studies.
chapters: A Book With a Bold Title

beats.scene: A man writes at a desk by lamplight in an old study
beats.summary: In 1910 Wallace Wattles published a short book with a bold promise about getting rich.

beats.scene: A busy street in 1910 with a tram, a telephone pole and new shops
beats.summary: The world of 1910 was full of new machines and new shops, and many people hoped to rise.

beats.scene: The title page of a small book lies open on a table
beats.summary: The title promises a science, which means Wattles says that getting rich follows fixed rules.

beats.scene: A busy worker reads a small book on a crowded train
beats.summary: In his preface Wattles says the book is a practical manual, not a theory for scholars.

beats.scene: A tired clerk reads by candlelight after a long day
beats.summary: He says busy people need short steps, not long arguments, so he keeps the book plain.

beats.scene: Old portraits hang above a long shelf of heavy books
beats.summary: He says his main idea is old and names thinkers such as Spinoza, Hegel and Emerson.

beats.scene: A man tests a plan at a workbench, checking each step
beats.summary: He says he has tested the method himself, which is his own claim and nothing a reader can check.

beats.scene: Three small boxes on a table hold three kinds of notes
beats.summary: This retelling sorts his ideas into good advice, personal beliefs and claims that need care.

beats.scene: A reader holds a small book whose chapters are marked with ribbons
beats.summary: The book has seventeen short chapters, and we follow them in order, some in several parts.

beats.scene: A young woman looks out of a window at a street of shops
beats.summary: Wattles begins with a question: is it even right to want to be rich?

beats.scene: A man in a bare room looks at a table with little on it
beats.summary: Wattles opens chapter one by saying that no one can live a full life without money.

beats.scene: A student bends over books and a lamp in a warm room
beats.summary: To grow in body, mind and spirit a person needs things to use, and things cost money.

beats.scene: A runner, a reader and a quiet worshipper stand in a bright hall
beats.summary: He says life has three sides, body, mind and spirit, and a full life uses all three.

beats.scene: A family sits at a plain table and shares a warm meal
beats.summary: He calls the wish for riches the wish for a richer, fuller and more abundant life.

beats.scene: A thin hermit in a dark cave turns away from a basket of fruit
beats.summary: He rejects the old idea that going without is holy, and calls the person who wants nothing abnormal.

beats.scene: A man hands a coin to a child at a market stall
beats.summary: He says a person with nothing can give little to others, so riches can be used for good.

beats.scene: A man in a fine coat looks down on a crowd from a balcony
beats.summary: He warns that the wrong reason is to rule over others or to show off.

beats.scene: A quiet couple walks through a garden at sunset
beats.summary: A modern reader will add that money does not guarantee happiness, and that many traditions praise simple living.

beats.scene: Two paths from a crossroads: one to a big house, one to a cottage
beats.summary: The book gives no figure for how much is enough, so each reader must decide what a full life needs.

beats.scene: A path leads from a small house toward hills in the morning light
beats.summary: If the wish is right, Wattles asks the next question: is there a sure way to reach it?

beats.scene: A teacher writes a sum on a chalkboard before a classroom
beats.summary: Chapter two states Wattles's main claim: there is a science of getting rich, as exact as arithmetic.

beats.scene: A man follows a clear line of footprints through fresh snow
beats.summary: He says certain laws govern getting rich, and anyone who follows them will succeed with the certainty of a sum.

beats.scene: Two shopkeepers stand outside neighbouring shops, one busy and one empty
beats.summary: He says where you live does not decide it, since people in one town get very different results.

beats.scene: A thrifty man counts coins into a jar beside a bare table
beats.summary: He says saving alone is not the answer, since many thrifty people stay poor.

beats.scene: A gifted painter sits in a bare room beside a plain, prosperous trader
beats.summary: He says talent is not the secret either, since many gifted people stay poor and some ordinary people grow rich.

beats.scene: A young man with an empty purse studies a plan in a small room
beats.summary: He says having no money at the start is not the real barrier, since some people grew rich from almost nothing.

beats.scene: A balance scale holds one coin in each dish, perfectly level
beats.summary: He says like causes always bring like effects, so the same actions should give the same results.

beats.scene: A man tends neat rows in a garden, a watering can beside him
beats.summary: He says anyone who does things in the Certain Way will get rich, on purpose or by accident.

beats.scene: A scientist weighs two small plants, one in sun and one in shade
beats.summary: A modern reader will say that real life has many causes, including luck, health, timing and where you start.

beats.scene: A young man with an open notebook sits at a desk, ready to learn
beats.summary: Wattles ends the chapter by saying that anyone can learn the way, and promises to teach it.

beats.scene: A worker stands before a tall locked gate in a high wall
beats.summary: Chapter three asks whether the rich have taken every chance, and Wattles says they have not.

beats.scene: One heavy door is shut but a wide door beside it stands open
beats.summary: He admits you may be shut out of one trade, but says that other trades stay open.

beats.scene: Early electric wires and a flying machine cross a bright sky over a town
beats.summary: New trades keep opening as old ones close, as electricity and flying machines were doing in his own day.

beats.scene: A crowd of workers walks out of a factory gate together
beats.summary: He says people stay poor not because they are robbed but because they do not yet do things in the Certain Way.

beats.scene: A great green valley with farms, forests, a river and a distant town
beats.summary: He says nature's supply is so large that it can never run out, so there is enough for everyone.

beats.scene: A farmer, a woodcutter and a miner look over land, forest and hills
beats.summary: He asks readers to look at the forests, fields and mines and see how much is still unused.

beats.scene: A farmer looks over cracked dry earth beside a nearly empty river
beats.summary: A modern reader must add that land, water and minerals are limited and that wealth is not shared equally.

beats.scene: A calm woman shares bread at a long table with plenty of food
beats.summary: He says that believing in plenty frees a person from the fear that makes people grab and hoard.

beats.scene: A boy gazes into a shop window full of fine things
beats.summary: His idea suggests a kinder way to see the rich: as proof that it can be done, and not as a loss to us.

beats.scene: A traveller stops at a signpost where roads lead in many directions
beats.summary: The door is open, Wattles says, and the next question is what the method itself rests on.

beats.scene: Stars shine over a quiet landscape with a dark hill and a lone house
beats.summary: Chapter four gives the first principle: Wattles says one thinking stuff fills the universe and makes all things.

beats.scene: A glowing mist spreads between stars, slowly drawing together into a sphere
beats.summary: In its first state, he says, the thinking stuff has no form, and every form comes from it.

beats.scene: Planets circle a bright sun in a dark sky
beats.summary: He says the stuff made the solar system by thinking of its form, and the system appeared.

beats.scene: A green forest where a deer and a bird move in morning light
beats.summary: He says it thought of plants and animals too, and living things slowly took form.

beats.scene: A person sits with closed eyes while a faint glow rises overhead
beats.summary: He says people can think in the same way, and that a thought held in this stuff can bring about the thing thought of.

beats.scene: Three numbered cards on a desk, each with a short line of writing
beats.summary: He sums up his belief in three steps and says the rest of the book stands on them.

beats.scene: A young man in a plain coat listens doubtfully as an older man speaks
beats.summary: He knows this sounds strange, and he invites readers to test the idea by its results.

beats.scene: An old philosopher in a robe points to ideas joined on a wall
beats.summary: Some philosophers have believed that everything is one thing in many forms, so Wattles is not alone.

beats.scene: A scientist in a laboratory looks through a microscope at a sample
beats.summary: Modern science has found no sign of a thinking stuff, and no proof that thoughts alone can make objects.

beats.scene: A man stands at a fork, one path lit by a lantern
beats.summary: He draws two lessons from his idea: the universe is friendly to growth, and what you think matters.

beats.scene: A seed splits open as a green shoot rises toward sunlight
beats.summary: Chapter five says that everything alive pushes to have more life, which Wattles calls the urge to increase.

beats.scene: A single seed in a hand and a field of ripe grain behind it
beats.summary: A seed planted in the ground gives many new seeds, so life spreads itself.

beats.scene: A boy at a school desk reads eagerly beside a pile of books
beats.summary: The mind grows in the same way: the more a person learns, the more they want to learn.

beats.scene: A woman at a window looks over a city, thinking of her hopes
beats.summary: He says our wish for more is the urge of life itself, working in us.

beats.scene: Sunrise over a wide landscape of fields, hills and a winding river
beats.summary: He says the power behind all things wants every person to have all they can use, so the universe is on your side.

beats.scene: A pianist sits at a fine piano in a bright room
beats.summary: He says life needs things to use, as a musician needs an instrument, so wanting things is part of living.

beats.scene: A crowd of different people walk together under a bright sky
beats.summary: He says the same urge works in everyone, so it is not selfish and no one is left out.

beats.scene: A woman stands tall and calm in a sunlit doorway
beats.summary: He tells readers they need not feel ashamed of wanting abundance, since the wish is part of life itself.

beats.scene: A balance with a coin on one side and a heart on the other
beats.summary: A modern reader will add that not every wish leads to good, and that more life is not always more money.

beats.scene: A traveller sets out on a bright road with a full backpack
beats.summary: Wattles concludes that the power is on your side, so a reader should drop doubt and learn how riches come.

beats.scene: A baker slides fresh loaves from an oven into a basket
beats.summary: Chapter six opens with a surprising claim: you do not have to take anything from anyone to get rich.

beats.scene: A crowded road where people push, beside a quiet open road
beats.summary: He describes two ways of living, the competitive plane and the creative plane, and urges the second.

beats.scene: Two men tug at one loaf of bread while a third bakes another
beats.summary: He says a mind set on winning and ruling is out of step with the creative power behind the world.

beats.scene: A baker sets a new loaf on a shelf, smiling at a customer
beats.summary: A baker who bakes a new loaf adds something to the world, and no one is robbed in the making of it.

beats.scene: A carpenter builds a new house on an empty plot of land
beats.summary: He says riches are made as well as moved around: a new house, book or machine adds to the world's wealth.

beats.scene: A man hides a heavy bag of coins under a floorboard, looking anxious
beats.summary: He says the creative person does not hoard or fear, because more can always be made.

beats.scene: A trader at a desk looks greedily at a heap of goods
beats.summary: He warns against the wish to get something for nothing, which has no place in the Certain Way.

beats.scene: Two shops face each other across a street, one with a crowded window
beats.summary: A modern reader will add that fair competition has its place, since rivals can push each other to improve.

beats.scene: A rich man helps a poorer neighbour up a hill, both smiling
beats.summary: He says the creative person is glad to see others rise, and the more who get rich this way, the better for all.

beats.scene: A traveller reads a signpost on a road leading to a busy town
beats.summary: To make your gain help others, he gives a rule about use value and cash value.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper hands a wrapped parcel to a smiling customer
beats.summary: Wattles gives his rule: give each person more in use value than you take from them in cash value.

beats.scene: A price tag hangs on a coat worn happily by a customer
beats.summary: Cash value is the price you take, and use value is the good the thing does for the buyer.

beats.scene: A boy cycles proudly along a country road on a new bicycle
beats.summary: As an example, a good bicycle costs a modest sum but may carry its owner to work for years.

beats.scene: A buyer and a seller shake hands, and both look pleased
beats.summary: He says every deal should add to life on both sides, so that each person goes away better off.

beats.scene: A craftsman checks the sturdy joints of a chair before selling it
beats.summary: His rule means that what you sell must be good, since you can only give use value that is real.

beats.scene: A merchant puts a false weight on his scale, and a customer frowns
beats.summary: He says cheating and tricks have no place in the Certain Way, which works only through fair dealing.

beats.scene: A trader names a fair price while a customer waits calmly
beats.summary: A fair reading of the rule is that both sides should gain, so a seller need not give everything away.

beats.scene: A farmer, a miller and a baker pass sacks of grain along a line
beats.summary: He says riches come through the usual channels of work and trade, not from some hidden source.

beats.scene: A house takes shape as builders lay bricks beside an architect's plan
beats.summary: He says a clear plan for a house will not raise walls by itself; it works through builders, shops and people.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper looks past one customer at a busy street of passers-by
beats.summary: He says to look to the great source for your supply, and to see each customer or employer as only a channel.

beats.scene: Hands folded in thanks beside a loaf of bread and a candle
beats.summary: Chapter seven names the first step: be thankful, which Wattles says keeps the mind close to the source of good.

beats.scene: A person at an open window greets the sunrise with raised hands
beats.summary: He says gratitude joins the mind to the thinking stuff, so that a person's thoughts are received.

beats.scene: A woman writes in a small notebook beside a cup of tea
beats.summary: He says the mind takes the form of what it dwells on, so thinking about good things makes the mind good.

beats.scene: A woman holds an old coat and smiles at its warmth
beats.summary: He says to be thankful for what you already have, even if it is small.

beats.scene: A man scowls at a bare table while others laugh over a meal
beats.summary: He says people who complain about what is wrong keep their minds fixed on poverty.

beats.scene: A person sits by a window with a hand resting on the heart
beats.summary: He says gratitude must be a real, lively and sincere feeling, and more than polite words.

beats.scene: A man writes three lines in a notebook by candlelight at night
beats.summary: He suggests spending free time in thankful thought, and a reader might write three good things each evening.

beats.scene: A woman gives a handwritten thank-you card to a smiling helper
beats.summary: Thanks to people count too: telling those who help you that you are grateful is part of good dealing.

beats.scene: A person sits quietly at a table with a bill, looking calm
beats.summary: A modern reader will add that gratitude helps mood and relationships but does not pay bills, and must not be used to silence people in need.

beats.scene: A reader finishes a list and looks up toward a bright window
beats.summary: Thanks is the foundation of the method, and the second step is to form a clear picture of what you want.

beats.scene: A man sits still with closed eyes, imagining a house with a garden
beats.summary: Chapter eight says to think in the Certain Way: form a clear mental picture of what you want.

beats.scene: A tangled ball of string beside a single straight line of thread
beats.summary: He says a vague wish is useless, since you cannot make a clear request from a cloudy idea.

beats.scene: A person sketches a small house with a garden and a blue door
beats.summary: He says to make the picture exact, with every detail, and to see the thing as if it were already yours.

beats.scene: A clock on a wall shows evening while a person sits deep in thought
beats.summary: He says to take time each day to go over the picture until it is fixed in the mind.

beats.scene: A sailor at a ship's wheel keeps one eye on a compass
beats.summary: Keep the picture in mind as a sailor keeps the harbour in view, whatever the weather does.

beats.scene: A woman writes three headings in her notebook: have, do and become
beats.summary: He says to be definite about what you want to have, to do and to become.

beats.scene: A boy leans forward at a shop window, wishing hard for a bicycle
beats.summary: A real wish matters, since a half-hearted idea will not hold the mind for long.

beats.scene: A student studies a list of goals pinned above a desk
beats.summary: Modern research finds that clear goals help people more than vague ones.

beats.scene: A girl runs toward a finish line, watching her feet on the track
beats.summary: Some researchers add that dreaming only of the prize can drain effort, so planning the steps matters too.

beats.scene: A reader checks a written goal against a short list of honest questions
beats.summary: A person should check that the picture shows something they truly want and that harms no one.

beats.scene: A traveller studies a map with a marked route to a distant city
beats.summary: He says a picture is not enough: you must have faith, and believe the thing is already on its way.

beats.scene: A man lays a table for a guest who has not yet arrived
beats.summary: He says to think of the thing as already yours, since in thought it is yours before it reaches your hands.

beats.scene: A grey cloud drifts away from a sunlit window where a woman stands
beats.summary: He says every doubt is a thought of not having the thing, so doubt must be put away.

beats.scene: Two friends whisper at a table while one looks away
beats.summary: He advises keeping your plans to yourself unless a listener believes in them.

beats.scene: A man hums cheerfully at a workbench, though the room is still bare
beats.summary: He says to give thanks for the thing in advance, as though it had already arrived.

beats.scene: A woman at a desk reads a letter with a calm, hopeful face
beats.summary: Psychologists find that people who trust they can do a task often keep trying longer.

beats.scene: A man studies a column of figures at a desk, calm but alert
beats.summary: Faith must not replace facts: a person who believes in a plan should still check the numbers.

beats.scene: A farmer waits calmly at the edge of a green young field
beats.summary: Faith needs patience too, because good things, like a crop, take time to grow.

beats.scene: A woman stands at a window at dawn, quiet and ready for the day
beats.summary: He says to return to the picture and the faith often, since one burst of effort is not enough.

beats.scene: A man grips the wheel of a small boat in a stiff wind
beats.summary: After picture and faith comes the will, and Wattles says what it is for and what it is not for.

beats.scene: A man stands firm on a rock while a river rushes past
beats.summary: Chapter nine says not to use your will on anything outside yourself.

beats.scene: A small figure pushes at a large mountain, which does not move
beats.summary: He says it is a mistake to push the universe by force of will, since there is no need.

beats.scene: A man tugs a woman's sleeve as she walks calmly away
beats.summary: He says you must not try to force other people with your will, because it is wrong.

beats.scene: A woman sits at a desk, writing a firm plan for the week
beats.summary: He says to use the will on yourself, to keep yourself thinking and acting in the Certain Way.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a long road, moving steadily on his own feet
beats.summary: A traveller reaches the end of a road by moving his own feet, not by pushing the road.

beats.scene: A man turns down a lamp and goes to bed at a fixed hour
beats.summary: Self-command means choosing what to think and do, even when your mood says something else.

beats.scene: A student plans study time with a small clock and a checklist
beats.summary: Psychologists find that willpower is helped more by habits and plans than by straining in the moment.

beats.scene: A seller listens patiently to a customer and lets her choose
beats.summary: To respect the free choice of others means you may offer good things, but never trick or press anyone.

beats.scene: A tired woman rests in a chair with her feet up and eyes closed
beats.summary: The will needs rest as well, since a tired mind is not firm; sleep, food and breaks all help.

beats.scene: A reader at a table puts down a newspaper full of gloomy headlines
beats.summary: Wattles also says what to keep out of your mind: poverty, and the gloomy talk about it.

beats.scene: A man turns his back on a heap of newspapers with grim headlines
beats.summary: He says not to study poverty or talk about it, but to think about riches instead.

beats.scene: A man waters a seedling beside a dry cracked patch of earth
beats.summary: His reasoning is that what you think about grows, so attention paid to poverty makes it larger.

beats.scene: A reader closes a gloomy book and opens a bright one by a window
beats.summary: He tells readers to avoid books and stories that dwell on misery or say the world is going to the bad.

beats.scene: A well-dressed woman points a poorer man toward a shop hiring workers
beats.summary: He says the best way to help the poor is to get rich yourself and show them it can be done.

beats.scene: A hand drops a coin into a thin man's hat on the street
beats.summary: He says a gift of money may ease a hard day, but only learning how to rise can end poverty.

beats.scene: A nurse, a teacher and a volunteer help people in a plain clinic
beats.summary: Most modern readers find this too simple: poverty has many causes, and people who face it directly have helped many.

beats.scene: A woman switches off a lamp beside a table of newspapers
beats.summary: The useful part is that constant bad news wears people down, so it is wise to choose what you take in.

beats.scene: A man looks up at a sunrise over hills with a hopeful face
beats.summary: Wattles is an optimist: he says the world is moving toward the good, and a hopeful outlook is natural.

beats.scene: A group of friends laughs together around a lamp-lit table
beats.summary: He says to turn away from gloomy talk and to seek hopeful people and hopeful ideas.

beats.scene: A woman walks from a crowded street into a quiet sunlit square
beats.summary: A person can care about others and still keep a hopeful mind, and the next chapter asks how to keep that hope steady.

beats.scene: A man walks steadily uphill toward a high bright peak
beats.summary: Chapter ten says the picture needs a steady purpose: the wish to get rich must be strong and must last.

beats.scene: A person looks past a stack of bills at a goal on the wall
beats.summary: When the facts around you look bad, he says to look past them to the picture and not treat the present as final.

beats.scene: A woman at a table sorts bills calmly, with a plan beside her
beats.summary: A wise reader faces the facts and keeps the aim: unpaid bills are real and have to be dealt with.

beats.scene: A driver keeps his eyes on a long road ahead, hands steady
beats.summary: He says to keep the mind on the goal each day, as a driver keeps his eyes on the road ahead.

beats.scene: A feeble wisp of smoke beside a firm stone pillar
beats.summary: A wish is weak and a purpose is a decision, and a wish becomes a purpose when a person commits to it.

beats.scene: A man at a mirror gives himself a steady, encouraging look
beats.summary: He tells readers to speak of themselves and their hopes in hopeful words, and never to call themselves failures.

beats.scene: An inventor holds a tiny glowing thread at a bench of many tried materials
beats.summary: Edison and his helpers tried a very large number of materials before they found a lasting thread for the light bulb.

beats.scene: A mother and father plan a garden while children dig nearby
beats.summary: He wants the purpose to fit a larger good: a person's aim should add to life, including the lives of others.

beats.scene: A man sleeps soundly in bed while a clock shows early morning
beats.summary: A steady mind also needs rest, food and friends, since stress can wear down even a strong purpose.

beats.scene: A man rolls up his sleeves and steps through a workshop door
beats.summary: All this thinking is useless without action, and Wattles's next chapter says so firmly.

beats.scene: A small boat strikes a rock near a rocky shore at dusk
beats.summary: Chapter eleven says thought is not enough: many thinkers are wrecked by failing to join thought to action.

beats.scene: A farmer with a plan and a plough crosses his field at dawn
beats.summary: He says thought should guide action, and the things you want will come through the work you do.

beats.scene: A clock above a busy workshop shows the present hour
beats.summary: He says you can act only in the present, not in the past and not in the future.

beats.scene: A young man stands in a small shop, looking over the counter
beats.summary: He says to act where you are, not where you were or where you would like to be.

beats.scene: A clerk waters a small plant on his desk in a plain office
beats.summary: He says not to wait for a better environment, because acting well on your present one is how a better one is made.

beats.scene: A woman with old tools mends a chair in a modest workshop
beats.summary: He says not to wait for a great chance, but to do what you can today with the tools you have.

beats.scene: A bookkeeper reads a manual at night beside a small lamp
beats.summary: A young clerk with no savings who learns every part of the shop is already preparing for a better position.

beats.scene: A man in a worn apron sketches a new shop while still at work
beats.summary: He says that a person in the wrong work should not wait for the right work, but do the present job well as a step.

beats.scene: A daydreamer gazes from a window while a pile of work waits behind him
beats.summary: Thought without action is only daydreaming, and a plan without a first step is only a wish.

beats.scene: A man tests a small bridge with one foot before crossing
beats.summary: A modern reader will add that acting now should be sensible: start small, test, learn, and risk only what you can afford.

beats.scene: A craftsman polishes a small wooden box at a bench
beats.summary: Chapter twelve says to do each day all that can be done that day, and to do each act well.

beats.scene: A tailor stitches a coat carefully, each stitch even and neat
beats.summary: He says to make each act a success in itself, since a successful life is made of successful acts.

beats.scene: A leaking bucket spills water as a man hurries along a path
beats.summary: He says a careless act is a loss that cannot be made up later, so do not put half your effort into anything.

beats.scene: A worker looks at a long list of tasks and picks the first one
beats.summary: He says not to try to do tomorrow's work today, since it is not the number of things you do but how well each is done.

beats.scene: A calm man walks briskly along a quiet road, not running
beats.summary: He says not to hurry or worry, and to keep a calm mind and a steady pace.

beats.scene: A man at a workbench glances up at a framed sketch of his goal
beats.summary: He says to keep the vision in mind while you work, so that each task serves the goal.

beats.scene: A man crosses another day off a wall calendar with a pencil
beats.summary: Success is built from small habits repeated every day.

beats.scene: A violin student practises a short passage again and again
beats.summary: Research on practice finds that skills grow through steady practice with honest feedback.

beats.scene: A woman reviews her day in a notebook at the end of the evening
beats.summary: A simple habit is to look back each evening and ask which acts were done well and which were not.

beats.scene: A man sleeps deeply, the lamp out and the window open to stars
beats.summary: A steady worker who rests does better than an exhausted one, since overwork harms health and judgment.

beats.scene: A young person studies tools of different trades hanging on a wall
beats.summary: Chapter thirteen says each kind of work needs its own talent, such as musical talent for a music teacher.

beats.scene: A gifted musician plays to an empty room; a shopkeeper counts coins
beats.summary: He says talent alone does not make a person rich, since there are skilled people who stay poor.

beats.scene: A woman with many tools on a table chooses one to start with
beats.summary: He says you may have many talents, and the best choice is the work you most wish to do.

A1A2: In 1910 a man named Wallace Wattles wrote a book about getting rich.
The world of 1910 was changing fast, with new machines and shops.
The title says science, so he thinks getting rich follows rules.
He says his book is a guide for action, not a long theory.
He says busy people need short steps, so his book is plain.
He says his big idea is old and comes from wise thinkers.
He says he tried the method himself and it worked for him.
In this book we will separate good advice from beliefs.
The book has seventeen short chapters, and we will read them in order.
Wattles starts with a simple question: is it wrong to want money?
Wattles says nobody can live a full life without some money.
To learn and grow, a person needs books, food and a warm home.
He says a full life uses the body, the mind and the spirit.
He says wanting riches means wanting a fuller and happier life.
He says going without is not holy, and wanting more is normal.
He says a person with nothing can give very little to others.
He says the wrong reason is to rule over others or to show off.
Money is useful, but it does not always make people happy.
He gives no number for how much is enough, so you must decide.
If the wish is right, is there a sure way to reach it?
He says getting rich is a science, like arithmetic.
He says certain rules decide who gets rich, and anyone can follow them.
He says place does not decide it, since neighbours get different results.
He says saving alone is not enough, as many careful people stay poor.
He says talent is not the secret, since many clever people stay poor.
He says a poor start does not stop you, because many began with nothing.
He says the same actions always give the same results.
He says anyone who uses the Certain Way will get rich.
Real life has many causes, including luck, health and timing.
He says anyone can learn the Certain Way, and he will teach it.
Some people say the rich have taken every chance, but Wattles disagrees.
One trade may be closed to you, but others are open.
New kinds of work keep appearing as old kinds end.
He says people stay poor because they do not use the Certain Way.
He says nature has plenty for everyone, and it will not run out.
Look at the land, he says, and see how much is unused.
But land and water are limited, and wealth is not shared equally.
He says believing in plenty frees you from fear and greed.
Other people's wealth can show you what is possible, not what is lost.
The door is open, he says, so now we learn the method.
He says one thinking stuff fills the whole world and makes all things.
At first, he says, this stuff had no shape at all.
He says the stuff thought of a solar system, and one appeared.
He says it thought of trees and animals, and they grew.
He says a person's thought, held in this stuff, can make things.
He gives three ideas: one stuff, thought makes things, and we can use it.
He knows this sounds strange, and he asks you to test it.
Some old thinkers also believed that all things are one.
Science has found no sign of a thinking stuff in nature.
Wattles says two things follow: life is friendly, and thoughts matter.
He says every living thing is always trying to grow more.
One seed in the ground can grow into many new seeds.
The mind grows too, and learning makes us want more learning.
He says our wish for more is life itself, working in us.
He believes the whole universe is on your side when you grow.
A musician needs an instrument, and life needs tools to express itself.
He says the same urge lives in everyone, so no one is left out.
He says you need not feel ashamed of wanting a better life.
Not every wish is good, and more life is not always more money.
He says the power is on your side, so put doubt away.
He says you do not have to take anything from anyone.
He describes two ways to live and tells us to choose the second.
He says a mind that only wants to win is out of step.
A baker makes a new loaf and no one is robbed.
New houses, books and machines add to the wealth of the world.
He says a creative person does not need to hoard or fear.
He warns against trying to get something for nothing.
Fair competition has a place too, because rivals help each other improve.
He says the creative person wants others to rise too.
To make your gain help others, Wattles gives a simple rule.
His rule is to give people more value than the money you take.
Cash value is the price, and use value is the good it does.
A good bicycle costs little but can serve its owner for years.
He says every deal should leave both sides better off.
You can only give real value, so what you make must be good.
He says cheating and tricks have no place in his method.
Both sides should gain, so you need not give everything away.
He says riches come through ordinary work and trade.
A plan for a house is built by builders, not by magic.
He says each customer is only one channel for your good.
He says the first step is to feel thankful.
He says thanks joins your mind to the source of all good.
He says the mind becomes like the things it thinks about.
He says to be thankful for what you already have.
He says people who always complain keep their minds on lack.
He says thanks must be a real feeling, not just words.
Each evening, you might write down three things you are thankful for.
Thank the people who help you, and tell them so.
Thanks helps us feel better, but it does not pay bills.
Thanks is the first step, and a clear picture is the second.
He says to form a clear mental picture of what you want.
A vague wish is weak, and a clear wish is strong.
He says to see every detail of what you want.
He says to spend time each day on your picture.
Keep your goal in mind, as a sailor watches the compass.
He says to decide what you want to have, do and become.
A real wish matters, because a weak idea soon fades.
Clear goals help people more than vague goals do.
Planning the steps matters as much as dreaming of the prize.
Check that your goal is truly yours and harms no one.
He says you also need faith that your goal is on its way.
He says to behave as if what you want is already coming.
He says doubt weakens the picture, so put doubt away.
He says do not share your plans with people who doubt.
He says to give thanks for it now, before it arrives.
People who believe they can do a task often try longer.
Faith does not replace facts, so you should still check the numbers.
Faith needs patience, because good things take time to grow.
He says to return to your picture and your faith every day.

He says do not use your will on things outside yourself.
He says you cannot push the world with force of will.
He says you must not force other people to do your will.
He says to use your will to keep yourself on track.
You move your own feet, and you do not push the road.
Self-control means choosing what to think, even when you are tired.
Plans and habits help the will more than hard straining.
You may offer good things, but you must never trick people.
A tired mind is not firm, so sleep and rest matter too.
Wattles also says what to keep out of your mind: poverty.
He says do not study poverty, but think about riches.
He thinks that what you think about grows larger.
He says avoid books that say the world is going bad.
He says you help the poor best by becoming rich yourself.
He says a gift can help today, but it cannot end poverty.
Most modern readers say poverty has many causes, not just thoughts.
Too much bad news can wear you down, so choose wisely.
Wattles is hopeful, and he believes the world is getting better.
He says to choose hopeful friends and hopeful talk.
You can care about others and still keep a hopeful mind.
He says you need a strong purpose that lasts.
He says to look past bad facts to your goal.
Bills are real, so face the facts and keep your aim.
Keep your mind on your goal, like a driver watching the road.
A wish is weak, but a firm purpose is strong.
He says to speak of your hopes in hopeful words.
Edison tried very many materials before his light bulb worked.
He wants your goal to add to life, including other people's.
A strong purpose still needs rest, food and good friends.
Thought alone is not enough, so action comes next.
He says thinking alone is not enough, and action is needed.
He says your thoughts guide your actions, and actions bring results.
He says you can only act now, not in the past.
He says to act where you are, not where you wish to be.
A better place comes from working well in the place you have.
He says do what you can today, with the tools you have.
A clerk who learns the whole shop is preparing for more.
If your job is wrong, do it well while you look further.
Thought without action is only a dream with no result.
Start small, test your idea, and risk only what you can lose.
He says to do all you can each day, and do it well.
He says to make every act a small success in itself.
He says a careless act is a loss you cannot get back.
He says it is not how much you do, but how well.
He says do not hurry or worry, but keep a steady pace.
He says to keep your goal in mind while you work.
Success is built from small habits repeated every day.
Skills grow best through steady practice and honest feedback.
Each evening, look back and ask which tasks you did well.
A rested worker does better work than a tired one.
He says each kind of work needs its own kind of talent.
Talent alone does not make anyone rich, he says.
He says to pick the work you most wish to do.
He says a strong wish to do something shows you can do it.
Many skills can be learned, so a lack of training need not stop you.
He says do not fear a wrong start, because you can change.
Ask what you enjoy, what you do well, and what people need.
He says to include your chosen work in your mental picture.
Not everyone can choose freely, because bills and duties matter.
Keep a steady job while you try new work, and ask for advice.
He says to give every person a sense of gain.
Each customer should feel they get more than they pay for.
He says your own faith and purpose can be felt by others.
It should show in your words, your letters and your manner.
He says people come back to a business that treats them well.
He says teachers and doctors should add to the lives of others.
A good teacher helps children feel that they are growing.
He says there can be no tricks, and the gain must be real.
Good service helps, but it does not guarantee success.
For employees the same idea takes another form, which comes next.
He says employees can rise, and he calls them advancing men.
He says to do more each day than you are paid for.
He says good employers want to keep people who keep growing.
He says to learn the next job before you have it.
He says do not wait for luck, but work toward your goal.
He says to work from faith, not from fear of losing the job.
Work hard, and also ask for training and fair pay.
Some employers do not reward extra effort, so use good judgment.
If there is no room to grow, move on calmly.
Step by step, a person can rise, one day at a time.
He knows some people will doubt him, and he invites tests.
If you fail, he says, you did not follow the method.
He says to read the book daily and avoid rival ideas.
The summary begins with the one thinking stuff and creative thought.
Next, be thankful, picture your goal clearly, and keep faith.
Then he says to act every day and do each act well.
He ends with fair dealing and a promise of riches.
Clear goals, honest work and a thankful heart are worth keeping.
But thoughts alone do not make things, and results are never certain.
Take what helps you, test it, and decide for yourself.
B1B2: In 1910 an American writer named Wallace Wattles published a short book with a bold promise. He said that any person could learn a certain way to become rich.
In 1910 the world was changing quickly, with railways, telephones and electric light spreading through towns. Many ordinary people hoped that these new times might also bring them a better life.
The word science usually means knowledge that has been tested and is exact. Wattles chose it because he believed that getting rich follows fixed rules, just as arithmetic does.
In his preface Wattles says that his book is practical and not philosophical. It is meant for people who want to get rich, and not for people who only want to study ideas.
Wattles knows that most of his readers are busy people with little free time. For that reason he keeps his sentences plain and his advice short.
Wattles says that his main idea is very old. He names thinkers such as Spinoza, Hegel and Emerson, who also wrote about the unity of all things.
Wattles says that he has tested his method in his own life and that it works. This is only his word, because the book gives no records or numbers that we can check.
As we read, we will sort Wattles's ideas into three kinds. Some are sensible advice, some are his personal beliefs, and some are claims that need careful thought.
After the preface, the book has seventeen short chapters. We will follow them in order, and the longer ones will be told in several parts.
Wattles begins with a question that makes many people uneasy. Is it right, or is it selfish, to want to be rich?
The first chapter begins with a plain but daring claim about money. Whatever people say in praise of poverty, Wattles says, nobody can live a full life without it.
To grow, Wattles says, a person needs many things to use. Food, clothes, books and a warm home all cost money, and so does the free time to enjoy them.
Wattles says that life has three sides, which are the body, the mind and the spirit. None is better than the others, and a person lives fully only when all three can be used.
Wattles says that the wish to be rich is really the wish for a richer, fuller and more abundant life. He thinks that this wish is natural, and that it deserves praise and not blame.
Wattles rejects the old idea that going without is holy. He says that a person who does not want enough to live well is not normal.
Wattles also says that being poor makes it hard to help other people. Someone with plenty can feed a hungry neighbour or support a school.
Wattles does warn against one particular kind of wish, and it is an important one. If you want riches only to show off or to rule over others, he says, you have the wrong reason.
Modern readers may want to add a gentle caution to this chapter. Money is useful, but it does not by itself bring happiness, health or good friends.
Wattles never says exactly how much money is enough. Each reader has to decide what a full life would need, and that is a useful question to ask.
Wattles has now argued that the wish is right. His next question is whether there is a sure way to reach it, and his second chapter says that there is.
The second chapter states the main claim of the whole book. Wattles says there is a science of getting rich, and that it is exact, like arithmetic.
Wattles says that certain laws decide who becomes rich. Anyone who learns and obeys them, he claims, will succeed with the certainty of a sum in arithmetic.
Wattles first says that the place where you live does not decide the matter. If it did, everyone in a rich town would be rich, but neighbours in the same street do very differently.
Wattles says that getting rich is not simply a matter of saving. Many careful people who spend very little still stay poor, he notes, while some free spenders grow rich.
Wattles says that talent is not the secret either. Many gifted people stay poor, he says, and many people of ordinary ability become rich.
Wattles says that having no money at the start is not the real barrier. Money makes growth faster, he says, but people with nothing have begun and still grown rich.
Wattles reminds us that like causes always bring like effects. So when two people do the same things in the same way, he says, they must get the same result.
Wattles says that anyone who does things in the Certain Way will get rich, whether on purpose or by accident. Anyone who does not will stay poor, however able that person may be.
Today we would say that real results have many causes, including luck, health, timing and where a person starts. A true science would also need tests, and Wattles offers none.
Wattles ends the chapter with a promise to the reader. The Certain Way can be learned by anyone who is willing to try, he says, and the rest of the book will teach it.
The third chapter asks whether the rich have taken all the opportunities. Some people believe so, but Wattles says that this is not true.
Wattles agrees that you may be shut out of some kinds of business. But when one door is closed, he says, many others remain open.
History shows that new trades keep opening as old ones close. In Wattles's own time, electric power and flying machines were only beginning to create new kinds of work.
Wattles says that people are not poor because the rich hold them down. They are poor, he claims, because they have not yet learned to do things in the Certain Way.
Wattles argues that nature has more than enough for everyone on the earth. He believes that the great supply from which all things come can never be used up.
Wattles asks his readers to look at the forests, fields and mines of the world. Most of what lies there, he says, has not yet been put to use.
Today we know that land, fresh water and many minerals are limited. We also know that wealth is shared very unequally, so the idea of plenty needs care.
Wattles believes that trust in plenty takes away fear. A person who is not afraid of running short, he says, has no need to grab or to hoard.
Wattles's idea leads to a kinder way of looking at rich people. Their success can be seen as proof that it can be done, and not as something taken from us.
Wattles has now argued that the door is open to everyone. Next he must explain what the method itself rests on, and his answer is his boldest idea.
The fourth chapter gives Wattles's first principle, which is the base of the whole book. He says there is one thinking stuff from which all things are made, and that it fills the whole universe.
In its original state, Wattles says, this stuff has no shape at all. Every form that we see in the world, from a leaf to a mountain, is made from it.
Wattles claims that the thinking stuff made the solar system by thinking of its form. Whatever the stuff thinks of, he says, takes shape and becomes real.
In the same way, Wattles says, the thinking stuff thought of plants and animals. Slowly, along the lines of natural growth, living things took the shape that it imagined.
Next comes the claim that matters most for his method. A thought held in the thinking stuff, Wattles says, can cause the thing imagined to be created.
Wattles sums up his belief in three short steps, which are easy to remember. There is one stuff, a thought in it makes the thing thought of, and a person can use this power.
Wattles knows that his idea sounds strange to many people. He asks the reader to try the method and to judge the idea by its results.
Some philosophers have long believed that everything is one thing in many forms. In this sense Wattles is repeating an old idea, though he adds his own bold claims.
Modern science has found no sign of a thinking stuff. It has also found no evidence that thoughts alone can make objects appear.
Wattles draws two important lessons from this first principle of his. The universe, he says, is friendly to growth, and the way a person thinks matters a great deal.
In chapter five Wattles says that every living thing is pushing to have more life. He calls this the urge to increase, and he sees it everywhere.
Think of a single seed planted in the ground. It grows into a plant that makes many more seeds, so that life spreads itself widely.
Wattles says that the mind grows in the same way as a seed. The more a person learns, the more that person wants to know about the world.
Wattles says that our wish for more is the urge of life itself. It is life trying to express itself more fully through each of us.
Wattles believes that the power behind all things wants you to have everything you can use. In his view, the whole universe is friendly to your plans.
A musician cannot make music without an instrument to play it on. In the same way, Wattles says, life needs things to use if it is to express itself fully.
Wattles says that the same urge to grow lives in everyone. For this reason, he says, the wish for a fuller life is not selfish and leaves no one out.
Wattles says that nobody needs to feel ashamed of wanting more from life. The wish is natural, and it comes from the same source as all growth.
Of course, not every wish is a good one, and wanting more can sometimes hurt us or others. Also, a fuller life may mean more friends, time or health, and not only more money.
Wattles concludes that the power of life is on your side. He asks you to put doubt away and to learn how riches actually come.
Chapter six begins with a surprising claim about how riches come. Wattles says that you do not have to take anything from anyone in order to get rich.
Wattles describes two ways of living and working, and he prefers the second. On the competitive plane people fight over a prize, but on the creative plane they make something new.
Wattles says that a mind set on beating others is out of step with the way life works. Life, he says, is always creating and never fighting over scraps.
Picture a baker who makes a new kind of loaf. She has made something that did not exist before, and nobody has been robbed to make it.
Wattles says that wealth can be made and not only moved from one pocket to another. A new house, a new book or a new machine adds to the wealth of the world.
Because more can always be made, Wattles says, the creative person has no need to hoard. Fear of losing things keeps a mind small and closed.
Wattles warns against the wish to get something for nothing. A person who tries to take more than they give, he says, has left the creative path.
A modern reader may add that fair competition is not always bad. Rivals can push each other to improve, and customers often gain from that.
Wattles says that the creative person is glad to see others rise. The more people who get rich in this way, he says, the better the world becomes.
Wattles has said that your gain should help other people as well. To show how, he gives a rule about use value and cash value.
Here is Wattles's rule for honest business, and it is the heart of his advice. You must give every person more in use value than you take from them in cash value.
Cash value is the price that a person pays. Use value is the good that the thing does for the person who has bought it.
Think of a good bicycle bought for a modest sum. It may carry its owner to work and back for years, so the use is far greater than the price.
Wattles says that every deal should add to the life of both people. Each person should walk away from the deal better off than before.
Wattles's rule has a plain and practical meaning for any seller. You can only give real use value if what you sell is good, so skill and quality matter.
Wattles says that cheating, false weights and clever tricks have no place in his method. In his view, only fair dealing can keep a person on the creative path.
A fair reading of the rule is that both sides should gain. A seller does not have to give everything away, only to give real value for the price.
Wattles says that riches do not drop from the sky. They come, he says, through the usual channels of work, trade and business.
Wattles says that your mental picture of a house will not raise walls by itself. Instead it works through builders, shops, banks and other people who do real work.
Wattles says to look to the great source for your supply, and not to any one customer or employer. Each of them, he says, is only a channel.
Chapter seven names the first step of the method. Wattles says it is gratitude, which he believes keeps a person's mind close to the source of all good.
Wattles claims that gratitude joins a person's mind with the thinking stuff. Without it, he says, the person's thoughts are not received.
Wattles says that the mind takes the form of whatever it dwells upon. A mind that thinks about good things therefore grows toward them.
Wattles says that you should be thankful for what you already have, even if it is small. A person who is not thankful for little, he says, will not be thankful for much.
Wattles says that people who complain about what is wrong keep their minds fixed on poverty. Their thoughts then shape what they notice and expect.
Wattles says that gratitude must be a real and lively feeling. Polite words said without feeling, he says, will not do the work.
Wattles suggests spending some free time each day in thankful thought. A simple way to do this is to write down three good things each evening.
Gratitude is not only a private feeling, because it can also be spoken to the people who help us. Telling them so is a kind habit and often a useful one.
Gratitude can improve mood and friendships, but it does not pay the bills. It should also never be used to tell a struggling person to stay quiet.
Thanks, then, is the first step of Wattles's method. The second step is to form a clear mental picture of what you want.
Chapter eight is about thinking in the Certain Way. Wattles says that you must form a clear mental picture of the thing you want.

Wattles says that the picture should be exact, down to the smallest detail. You should see the thing as though it were already in your hands.

Wattles says that you should give thanks for the thing in advance. Thanks are to be given as if the gift had already arrived.

Wattles says that the will has one proper use. It is to keep yourself thinking and acting in the Certain Way.
A traveller reaches the end of a road by moving his own feet. He does not do it by pushing the road itself.
Self-control means choosing what to think and do even when your mood says something else. It is a skill, and like other skills it grows with practice.

Respecting other people's free choice is part of his rule. You may offer good things in business, but you must never trick or press anyone.
A tired mind cannot hold a purpose firmly for very long. Good sleep, regular meals and breaks all make self-control easier.

Wattles says that you should not study poverty or talk about it. To get rid of poverty, he says, think about riches.
Wattles believes that whatever you think about tends to grow larger in your life. Attention paid to poverty, he says, only makes it bigger.
Wattles tells his readers to avoid gloomy books and articles that say the world is going to the bad. He thinks that they fill the mind with the wrong pictures.
Wattles says that the best way to help the poor is to get rich yourself. Your example, he says, shows them that it can be done.
Wattles says that gifts of money may ease a hard day. Only knowing how to rise, he believes, can end a person's poverty for good.
Most modern readers find this advice far too simple to be true. Poverty has many causes, such as illness, low pay, war and unfair treatment, and thinking alone cannot remove them.
The useful part of the advice is that constant bad news can wear a person down. It is wise to choose what you read and watch.
Wattles is a cheerful optimist about the world and its future. He believes that the world is slowly moving toward the good, and that a hopeful outlook is the sensible one.

Chapter ten returns to the use of the will, and it is about faith and purpose. Wattles says that the wish to get rich must be strong, and that it must last.

Think of a driver who keeps his eyes on the road ahead. In the same way, Wattles says, the mind must be kept on the goal each day.
A wish is a passing thing, but a purpose is a decision. A person turns a wish into a purpose by committing to it and to the steps that it needs.
Wattles tells readers to speak of themselves and their hopes in hopeful words. A person who keeps calling himself a failure, he says, will find it hard to rise.
Thomas Edison and his helpers tried a very large number of materials before they found a thread that glowed for long. Without a stubborn purpose, he might have stopped far too soon.
Wattles wants the purpose to fit with a larger good. A person's aim should add to life, including the lives of other people.
A steady mind needs rest, healthy food and good friends. Constant stress can wear down even the strongest purpose.
Wattles has now said how to hold the picture and the purpose. His next chapter says that all this thinking is useless without action.
Chapter eleven is about acting in the Certain Way. Wattles says that many thinkers fail because they never connect their thought with action.
Wattles says that thought should guide action, and that action should follow thought. The things you want, he says, will come to you through the work that you do.
Wattles says that a person can only act in the present. The past is over, and the future has not arrived.

Wattles says that you should not wait for a better environment. You make a better one by acting well on the one you have now.
Wattles says not to wait for a great opportunity. Do what you can today, with the tools that you already have.

A modern reader will add that acting now should also be sensible. It is wise to start small, to test an idea and to risk only what you can afford to lose.
Chapter twelve is about efficient action, and it makes two demands. Wattles says that you must do all that can be done each day, and do each act well.

Wattles says that a careless act is a loss that cannot be made up later. A person should never put half of his effort into anything.

Wattles says that you should keep your vision in mind while you work. Each small task then becomes a step toward the goal.

A simple habit can help a great deal, and it takes only a few minutes each evening. Look back over the day and ask which acts were done well and which were not.
Rest matters too, because a rested worker does better work than a tired one. Studies have linked long periods of poor sleep with worse judgment and worse health.

Wattles says that talent alone does not make anyone rich. There are very gifted musicians, blacksmiths and carpenters who stay poor.
Wattles says that a person may have many talents. The best choice, he says, is the work that you most want to do.
Wattles says that a strong desire to do a thing is a sign of the power to do it. The wish, he believes, is the ability asking for a way to be used.
A lack of training need not stop a person from trying. Many skills can be learned with time, effort and good teachers.
Wattles says that you should not be afraid of choosing wrongly. If you make a mistake, he says, you can change course.
A useful way to choose is to ask three questions. What do I enjoy, what am I good at, and what do other people need?
Wattles says that the kind of work you hope for should be part of your mental picture. The vision then includes what you want to do, and not only what you want to own.
Not everyone is free to choose their own work, and this is worth admitting. Bills, family duties and the jobs that exist in one's town all limit what a person can do.
A sensible plan is to keep a steady income while you try something new. It also helps to talk to people who already work in that field.
Chapter fourteen is about the impression of increase, which means a feeling of gain. Wattles says that whatever your work is, you should make people feel that they are gaining.
Wattles says that each customer should feel that they are getting more than they pay for. This feeling must be true, and not a trick of clever talk.
Wattles says that the sense of increase comes from the giver's own faith and purpose. People, he says, can feel it in a person's manner.
Wattles says that the sense of increase should show in everything you do. It should be felt in your words, your letters, your manner and your handling of every task.
Wattles says that people are drawn to the person who gives them a sense of gain. Customers who feel well treated come back and tell their friends.
Wattles says that the same rule applies to teachers, doctors and ministers. They should add to the life of every person they serve.
Think of a teacher whose pupils feel they are growing in skill and confidence. That is the kind of increase that Wattles has in mind, and money measures it poorly.
The sense of increase must be real and not the product of clever words or loud promises. A seller who makes false claims is deceiving the customer, and in the end himself.
Good service is a sound foundation, but it does not guarantee success. Price, timing, location and competition all matter too, and a kind business can still fail.
Wattles has spoken to owners of shops and businesses. In the next chapter he speaks to the employee, who may feel that the whole idea is meant for someone else.
Chapter fifteen is for people who work for others. Wattles says that you need not stay in your place, and he calls the one who grows the Advancing Man.
Wattles says that an Advancing Man does more each day than he is paid for. He gives more use value than the wage that he receives.
Wattles says that an employer will not want to lose a person who grows. If this one will not reward growth, he says, another will.
Wattles says that you should prepare for the next position before you have it. Learn the skills of the next level of work, so that you are ready when the chance comes.
Wattles says that the Advancing Man does not sit and wait for luck or for favours from others. He works toward his picture each day, and he lets the work speak for him.
Wattles says that the work should come from faith and purpose, and not from fear of being dismissed. Fear, he believes, makes a person smaller and more careless in his work.
Today we would add that extra effort should go with asking. A worker can ask for training, for new tasks and for fair pay.
Some employers do not reward extra effort, and that is worth admitting. Doing more for nothing, year after year, can simply be unfair, so a wise worker uses judgment.
When there is no more room to grow, Wattles says, the Advancing Man may move on. He leaves calmly and without bitterness, and he keeps the good name that he has earned.
Step by step, and one day at a time, an employee can rise. Wattles now turns to his closing chapters, which gather cautions and a summary of the whole method.
In chapter sixteen Wattles expects that many people will sneer at the idea of a science of getting rich. His reply is that readers should try the method and judge it by the results.
Wattles says that if a person fails, the fault lies in the doing and not in the method. A modern reader will see a problem, because a claim that can never be wrong cannot really be tested.
Wattles says to read his book every day and to keep it with you. He also says not to read rival systems of thought until the method has been tried.
Chapter seventeen sums up the method in a list of short statements. It begins with the thinking stuff, and with the idea that a person must pass from the competitive mind to the creative one.
The summary goes on to gratitude and to the clear mental picture. A person must be sincerely thankful, form a clear and definite picture of what he wants, and hold it with faith.
Next the summary says that the creative power works through the usual order of trade and growth. A person must therefore act every day and do each act in an efficient way.
The summary ends with use value above cash value and the impression of increase. Wattles promises that riches will come in proportion to a person's vision, purpose, faith and gratitude.
Some of Wattles's advice holds up very well when we test it against experience. Clear goals, thankfulness, steady daily work, honest service and a hopeful mind are all worth keeping.
Other claims do not hold up nearly so well under a careful look. Thoughts alone do not create objects, and no method can promise certain results, so a sensible reader makes plans and asks for advice.
Wattles died in 1911, only a year after his book appeared, yet people still read it today. Take what is useful, test it in your own life, and decide for yourself what is true.
C1C2: In 1910 an American writer named Wallace Wattles published a short and confident book whose title sounded almost like a laboratory report. Its promise was simple and bold: that anyone who followed a certain method could become rich, whatever his or her starting point. We will read it as Wattles wrote it, as a set of beliefs and advice that readers have argued over for more than a hundred years.

When Wattles wrote, factories, railways and telephones were changing how people worked, and electric light was reaching more and more homes. Shops and businesses were multiplying, and a young clerk or a farm worker could look at all this growth and wonder how to take a share. It was into this hopeful and restless world that his little book was sent out to find its readers.

To most of us the word science suggests careful tests, measurement and results that anyone can repeat. Wattles used it more loosely, since he wished to say that getting rich follows fixed laws and is not a matter of luck. Whether his book deserves the name is a question we will keep in mind as we read.

In a short preface, Wattles announces that his book is a practical manual and not a treatise on theories. He writes for the person who wants to get rich and has little patience for long arguments about why the method works. His promise is that those who follow the steps will see results, and he asks to be judged on that.

Wattles imagines his reader as someone who works all day and has only a few precious hours left in the evening. He therefore chooses plain words, short chapters and clear steps, in the hope that the advice can be remembered and used. This plainness is one reason the book has stayed in print for so long.

In the preface Wattles explains that the idea at the heart of his book is far from new, and he traces it through Eastern thought to European philosophers such as Spinoza and Hegel and to the American writer Emerson. These thinkers believed, each in his own way, that all things share one underlying nature. Wattles claims only to have turned their long and difficult arguments into advice that an ordinary reader can use.

Wattles tells his readers that he did not merely theorise, for he has tried the method himself and found that it succeeds. We should treat this as a sincere personal claim and nothing more, since the book offers no records, accounts or figures that anyone could examine. A fair reader can admire the confidence while still asking politely but firmly for some evidence.

This retelling keeps Wattles's boldest ideas, but it will not pretend that they are all equally sound. Where he gives sensible, practical advice we will say so, and where he states a personal belief we will call it a belief. Where a claim goes beyond what anyone can prove, we will add a gentle word of caution.

The book proper is built from seventeen brief chapters, each of which takes up a single step of the argument. We will walk through them in order, giving the larger ideas more room so that you can see exactly how Wattles builds his case. Along the way we will pause to say what seems wise and what seems doubtful.

Before he offers any method, Wattles faces the question that makes many honest people uneasy about money. Is it noble, or is it greedy, to want to be rich at all? His answer, which opens the first chapter, is bold and clear, and it is where our story really begins.

Wattles opens his first chapter with a statement that is meant to shock the modest and the pious. Whatever may be said in praise of poverty, he insists, no one can rise to his full height of talent and character without having plenty of money. For him this is not greed but a plain fact about how the world is arranged.

Wattles reasons that the mind cannot develop without books, teachers and leisure, and that the body cannot thrive without good food, clothing and a warm home. Each of these things must be bought in a society that runs on money. A person who has little of it, he concludes, has little room to grow.

In Wattles's view, a human being lives in three ways at once, through the body, through the mind and through the spirit. He does not rank them, and he thinks that a life confined to only one of the three is a life sadly diminished. To use all of them freely, he says, requires tools, leisure and comforts that money provides.

The heart of the chapter is a single claim, that the desire for riches is really the desire for a richer, fuller and more abundant life. Because wanting more life is the most natural wish in the world, Wattles concludes, it deserves praise and not blame. Here, as often in his book, he turns a word that sounds selfish into one that sounds almost sacred.

Some traditions have praised poverty as a path to holiness, and Wattles argues against them with some force. He calls the refusal to want a better life a kind of abnormality, as if a plant were to refuse the sun. His quarrel is with the belief that need is a virtue, and not with the many people who choose a simple life with open eyes.

Wattles adds a moral point to his practical one, for he believes that a person with nothing has little to give. It is easier to feed a hungry neighbour, support a school or comfort a sick friend when one's own needs are met. In his eyes, then, to become rich in the right spirit is also to become more useful to others.

Wattles does not approve of every motive, and he warns readers that the wish to dominate other people or to dazzle them with display is the wrong reason for wanting wealth. The right reason, in his view, is the growth of a fuller and freer life, both for oneself and for others. This distinction matters a great deal, because it separates his teaching from plain greed and from the mere love of display.

A modern reader will want to add a gentle caution to this chapter, for money is certainly useful but it cannot buy everything that makes a life good. Health, friendship, purpose and peace of mind often matter as much as income, which is why many traditions praise a simple life. The sensible view may be that money is a tool for living well and never the goal itself.

Notice that Wattles does not give a figure for what it means to be rich, and perhaps he was wise to leave it open. Each reader must decide how much money a full life would really require, and what it would be for. Answering that question honestly may be the best first step, whatever one thinks of the rest of his teaching.

Having argued that the wish to be rich is natural and good, Wattles turns to the practical question of how it might be fulfilled. His second chapter makes a daring answer, for it claims that there is a definite way, which can be learned like any other skill. Whether the claim is true is exactly what the rest of the book will help us to judge.

In his second chapter Wattles lays down the claim on which everything else depends. There is, he says, a science of getting rich, and it is as exact as arithmetic or algebra. If he were right, success with money would no longer be a lottery but a skill that anyone could learn.

According to Wattles, there are certain laws which govern the process of getting rich, and anyone who learns and obeys them must succeed. He compares the result to a sum, which always comes out the same when the steps are followed correctly. He calls this procedure the Certain Way, and most of his book is an attempt to describe it.

The first thing Wattles rules out is environment, for he notes that people in the same town and the same trade have very different fortunes. If the place decided the outcome, he reasons, everyone in a prosperous town would prosper and everyone in a poor district would stay poor. Since this plainly does not happen, he concludes that something else must be at work.

Neither is thrift the secret, Wattles argues, for he notes that many very careful people remain poor while some free spenders become rich. To his mind this shows that the difference lies in the way a person thinks and acts, and not in the habit of counting coins. A modern reader may reply that saving is wise, and so it is, but he is right that it is not enough by itself.

Nor is talent the key, in Wattles's opinion, because he observes that many brilliant people never prosper while others of quite ordinary ability grow wealthy. He suggests that anyone who studies the rich will find them to be an average lot, and not much cleverer than the rest of us. What they have in common, he says, is that they do certain things in a certain way.

Wattles also denies that a lack of capital keeps people poor, since he points out that many who now have wealth began with almost nothing. Money in hand makes the early steps easier, he admits, but he thinks that the person without it can still begin and grow. Modern readers will notice that this is the claim most in need of care, because a good start in life does help a great deal.

The reasoning behind the whole book is simple, for Wattles believes that like causes always produce like effects. If a person does what the rich do, in the way that the rich do it, he argues, then that person must receive the same reward. The weak point, of course, is the word like, since it is rarely possible to repeat a cause exactly.

Everything comes down, for Wattles, to the Certain Way, and he says that whoever follows it will get rich, whether on purpose or by accident. Those who do not follow it will remain poor, however hard they work and however gifted they may be. It is a bold promise, and he offers it without any hint of exceptions.

Here a modern reader should speak up, for in real life results have many causes, among them luck, health, timing, education and the circumstances of one's birth. A true science would also need careful tests that others could repeat, and Wattles offers none, only his own word and his own conviction. His method may still contain useful habits, but it should not be taken as a law like gravity.

The chapter closes on a note of encouragement, for Wattles insists that the Certain Way is open to anyone who is willing to learn it. It does not depend on birth, rank or special gifts, he says, only on a person's willingness to think and to act in the right manner. With that promise made, he turns to the doubt that might otherwise stop a reader at the door.

Chapter three takes up a bitter complaint, namely that the wealthy have fenced off every opportunity and left nothing for anyone else. Wattles will not accept it, and he argues that no person is kept poor merely because others have taken the chances first. Readers who have felt shut out may find this encouraging or too easy, depending on their own experience.

Wattles does not deny that a person may be shut out of a particular line of business, since some trades are held tightly by those already in them. He insists, however, that when one door is closed a great many others stand open, and that a wise person looks for those instead of staring at the locked one. The advice is practical, even if the doors are heavier for some people than for others.

As old industries decline, new ones are born, and the story of trade has always been a story of doors opening in unexpected places. In Wattles's own day electric power, motor cars and the first flying machines were beginning to create kinds of work that no one had imagined a generation earlier. Each such change gave newcomers a chance to enter at the very start, with nothing but their wits and their willingness.

A passage that many readers find harsh holds that working people are kept poor not by the rich but by their own failure to act in the Certain Way. Wattles believes that if enough of them learned the method, no power could hold them back. History suggests that the truth is more tangled, since laws, wages, health and chance also play their part.

Wattles is struck by the sheer abundance of the world, and he declares that there is more than enough for everyone.
