All things are made, he believes, from one great living supply, and he says that this supply cannot be exhausted. It is a generous vision, and it has a certain beauty, though it asks more of us than the facts can give.

Look at the forests, the fields, the mines and the seas, Wattles invites us, and consider how much of their riches has never been touched. The earth in his day was far from fully used, and he draws from this the lesson that no one need fear a shortage. As a picture of the world it was inviting, although it left out the limits that we now know to be real.

A modern reader has to add a necessary correction, for we now know that fresh water, fertile land and many minerals are limited and sometimes badly overused. We also know that wealth is shared very unevenly, and that a world with plenty in total can still leave many people in need. The idea of plenty is a hope worth holding, but it should be held alongside good planning and care for the earth.

The practical value of the idea, in Wattles's view, is that it removes fear, which is the root of much grasping. A person who truly believes that there is enough has no reason to snatch, to hoard or to take advantage of a neighbour. Even a sceptic may grant that people who feel secure are generally more generous and more willing to cooperate.

This view leads to a gentler way of looking at the wealthy, for their success need not be a reproach to everyone else. It can instead be read as evidence that the thing can be done, and as a reason for hope rather than for envy. Whether or not one accepts the theory behind it, envy is a poor guide, and hope costs nothing.

With the question of opportunity settled to his own satisfaction, Wattles can now turn to the foundation of the whole method. What he is about to say is the boldest idea in the book, and also the one that is hardest to defend. We will hear it exactly as he states it, and then ask what we can and cannot make of it.

Chapter four is the foundation of the book, and Wattles states his first principle without apology. There is, he says, one thinking stuff from which all things are made, a living material that fills every corner of the universe, including the spaces between the stars. Everything we see, on his account, is this single stuff wearing a particular shape.

In its original state, Wattles writes, the thinking stuff is formless, which is to say that it has no shape, colour or limit. Every shape that we see, from the smallest leaf to the largest mountain, he calls a form into which the stuff has moved. It is a picture that has something in common with ancient ideas of a single source behind all things.

In Wattles's account, the thinking stuff did not build the heavens with tools or with effort but simply thought of them. It thought of a solar system, he says, and the sun and the planets moved into their places. This is a belief about origins that comes from philosophy and faith, and it is not something that astronomy has ever found.

The same thinking stuff, Wattles goes on, thought of plants and animals, and life took shape slowly, along the lines of natural growth. Each living thing is, in his eyes, a thought that has taken a body. Scientists explain the origin of life very differently, by chemistry and by evolution over an immense span of time, and the two views are not easy to join.

From these beginnings Wattles draws the claim that carries the weight of his whole book. A person can form things in thought, he says, and by impressing that thought upon the formless stuff can cause the thing to be created. If this were true, the mind of every reader would be a kind of workshop, and imagination would be a tool as real as a hammer.

Wattles gathers his belief into three plain propositions, which he treats as the foundation for everything that follows. First, there is one thinking stuff; second, a thought in that stuff produces the thing thought of; and third, a human being can shape such thoughts and so cause things to appear. The rest of the book, as he sees it, is simply instruction in how to use that power.

Wattles is aware that a stranger might find all this unlikely, and he invites the reader to test the idea instead of merely arguing about it. What he asks is that the reader act as though the idea were true and judge it by what follows. That sounds fair, but it overlooks a difficulty, for results that come slowly and with many causes are hard to credit to a single belief.

Philosophers in many lands have held that all things are, at bottom, one thing, which appears to us in countless forms. In this sense Wattles is repeating an ancient idea, and a reader who likes that idea may find his chapter familiar and even beautiful. What is new is his claim that a person can use this oneness as a practical tool for making money.

It must be said plainly that science has not found any thinking stuff filling the universe, and it has no evidence that thoughts alone can bring objects into being. Physics studies matter, energy and forces, and none of these behaves as Wattles describes. A reader may value the idea as a belief or a poetic image, but should not mistake it for established fact.

From his first principle Wattles draws two lessons that will occupy him for much of the book. The first is that the whole of nature is friendly to growth and to the person who seeks it, and the second is that the quality of a person's thinking has real consequences. The second lesson, at least, can be accepted by almost anyone, whatever they believe about the universe.

Chapter five begins with what feels like a plain observation, that every living thing is driven to have more life. Wattles calls this force the urge to increase, and he sees it at work in the smallest seed and in the largest city. He is on firmer ground here than in the last chapter, for growth is certainly one of the great facts of living things.

Consider a single grain of wheat dropped into the earth, which wakes, grows and in time gives back many new grains. In this small example Wattles sees the whole principle of life, which does not simply hold its place but multiplies itself. Farmers have always depended on the fact, and so have all of us who eat bread.

The mind, Wattles argues, follows the same pattern as the seed, for every fact that we learn tends to make us curious about the next one. A child who has mastered a skill soon wants to try a harder one, and an adult who has enjoyed a good book goes looking for another. Nobody, it seems, is built to stand still for long, and Wattles takes this restlessness to be the very pulse of life.

When we long for a better home, a richer education or a freer way of living, Wattles says, we are feeling the urge of life itself. He believes that this longing is not a flaw in human nature but the very engine that drives all growth. It is a comforting reading of ambition, and it makes shame about wanting more look rather foolish.

From all this Wattles concludes that the power behind all things wishes every person to have everything he or she can use. The universe, he says, is friendly to our plans and wants us to prosper, so that we need not argue with it or beg it for favours. Believers will see in this a loving creator, while others will see only a hopeful way of speaking about nature.

Think of a violinist who has no violin, for she cannot make the music that lives inside her. Wattles applies the same logic to every human gift, saying that life needs things to use if it is to express itself in full. Wanting those things, he concludes, is part of living and not a betrayal of it.

Because the same urge lives in every person, Wattles argues, the power behind it cannot be partial or play favourites. It wants all people to flourish, and your own growth does not have to be bought at the expense of anyone else. This is one of the kindest parts of his teaching, and it fits well with his later advice to deal fairly.

Wattles wants his readers to put away any shame about their desires, for in his view a wish for abundance is simply life asking to be lived more fully. A person who has been taught to feel guilty about ambition may find real relief in this thought. The relief is genuine, even though the idea still has to be balanced with honesty and good sense.

A thoughtful reader will notice that the urge to increase is not always benign, since some wishes harm the person who holds them and many harm others. A fuller life may also mean more time, more friends or better health, and not merely a larger income. There is a further danger in the idea that the universe wants us to have things, because it can make people who struggle feel that they have somehow failed.

Wattles concludes that the power which moves all living things is on the side of anyone who reaches for a fuller life. He asks the reader to set aside doubt and to move on to the practical question of how riches actually arrive. That question occupies his sixth chapter, and it is here that his advice becomes most specific.

Chapter six explains how riches come to a person, and Wattles opens it with a surprising claim. You do not have to take anything from anyone, he says, in order to get rich, and you do not have to beat anybody to do so. The whole chapter rests on the difference between making things and merely taking them.

Wattles describes two ways of living, which he calls the competitive plane and the creative plane. On the first, people struggle against one another for a limited prize, and on the second they bring new things into the world. He urges the reader to live on the creative plane, and much of his advice in this chapter is a description of how to do so.

A mind that is always trying to win and to rule over others, Wattles says, is out of harmony with the great intelligence behind the world. That intelligence, he believes, is creative by nature and never competitive in spirit, so that a person who wishes to share its power must learn to think in the same way. A reader need not accept the theology to see that constant rivalry can be tiring and narrowing.

Picture a baker who bakes a new kind of loaf and sells it to people who are glad to have it. She has made something that did not exist before, and no one has been robbed in the making of it. This, in simple form, is the kind of getting rich that Wattles has in mind when he speaks of creating and not competing.

Wealth, Wattles insists, is something that can be made, and not merely something that is moved from one pocket to another. A new house, a new book, a better tool or a useful service adds to the stock of good things in the world, and those who make them have taken from no one. Economists would agree with the general point, since trade and invention have indeed made the world far richer than it once was.

A person who lives on the creative plane, Wattles says, is not afraid of running short, and so has no reason to hoard what he has. He knows that more can always be made, and so he can spend and give without alarm. Wise people have often noticed that fear of loss narrows the mind, and Wattles is surely right that it makes poor decisions.

Wattles warns his readers against the old dream of getting something for nothing, whether by trickery, by gambling or by simple greed. A person who tries to take more than he gives, he says, has left the creative plane and returned to the struggle of the competitive one. The warning is sound whatever one thinks of his philosophy, since many schemes that promise easy riches end in loss.

A modern reader may want to add that honest competition has real benefits, since rivals push one another to improve and customers often gain from the contest. Wattles's contrast works best as a contrast of attitudes, between the person who is trying to build something and the one who is merely trying to beat someone. Seen in that light, it is wise advice and not a ban on healthy rivalry.

The person who lives on the creative plane, says Wattles, is glad to see other people rise, and does not view their success as a loss. He believes that the more people there are who get rich by making and giving, the richer the whole world becomes. This optimistic idea echoes through the whole book, and it softens what might otherwise sound like a selfish message.

If riches are to be made without taking from others, then something must be given back in every deal, and Wattles knows it. He therefore offers a simple rule about what he calls use value and cash value, which he regards as the heart of honest business. To that rule we now turn, for it is one of the most useful ideas in the whole book.

Here is the rule at the centre of Wattles's advice about business, and the idea to which he returns most often. You must give every person more in use value than the cash value you receive from him, so that each deal leaves the other person better off. It is simple to state, and difficult to follow when we are tired, hurried or tempted to cut corners.

Cash value is simply the price on the label, the sum of money that changes hands in the shop. Use value, as Wattles means it, is the good that the thing does for its owner over time, in comfort, knowledge, convenience or delight. A wise seller tries to see that the second always runs ahead of the first.

Take as an example a sturdy bicycle that is bought for a modest sum and then carries its owner to work, to market and to visit friends for many years. The cash that changed hands was spent once and soon forgotten, but the use goes on day after day. This is exactly the kind of exchange that Wattles wants the honest seller to aim for.

Every transaction, Wattles says, should make for more life, so that both the buyer and the seller walk away better off than they came. A deal in which one side gains and the other loses does not belong to the creative plane, however legal it may be. It is a standard that most of us would be glad to find in every shop we enter.

The rule carries an obvious consequence, which is that the goods and services we offer must really be good. A seller cannot give value that he does not possess, and so the honest pursuit of riches is also a pursuit of skill, care and quality. In this respect Wattles points us toward habits that any employer or customer would admire.

Cheating, false promises and clever tricks, Wattles says, have no place in the Certain Way, because they take value from other people instead of adding it. A seller who deceives a buyer has left the creative plane, whatever profit he may make that day. Honest people have always known this, and it is pleasant to find it written so firmly in a book about getting rich.

A fair reading of the rule is that both sides should gain, and not that the seller must ruin himself for the benefit of the buyer. A business that loses money on every sale soon disappears and then serves no one at all. The aim is a fair exchange in which the customer receives real value and the seller receives an honest return.

Wattles is careful to say that riches do not drop out of the sky or appear by magic, but come through the usual channels of work, trade and business. The creative power, as he describes it, works along the lines of natural growth and the existing order of society. This is a sensible correction to the more dreamy ideas that some readers may take from the early chapters.

Suppose that you hold in mind a clear plan for a house, and do not expect walls to rise of their own accord. The thing you want, Wattles says, will come through builders, suppliers, banks and the ordinary traffic of trade, so you must be ready to take part in all of it. In plain terms, the idea sets a direction, but the journey is made on foot.

Wattles advises his readers to look to the great source for their supply, and never to rest their hopes on any single customer or employer. Each of these people, he says, is merely a channel through which good things may flow, and the loss of one channel need not alarm anyone. Practical people will notice a sound lesson here, which is not to depend on one customer or one boss for everything.

Chapter seven names the first step in the practice of the method, and the step is thankfulness. Wattles believes that a mind which is truly grateful stays close to the source of all good, and that a mind which is ungrateful drifts away from it. Whatever we make of the metaphysics, the habit of gratitude has found many friends among thoughtful people.

In Wattles's theory, gratitude is the link that joins the mind of the person to the intelligence of the thinking stuff. Without that link, he says, a person's thoughts and wishes are not received, and the whole method stands idle. This is a claim of belief, and the reader should hold it as such, even while appreciating its call for a thankful spirit.

The mind, Wattles says, takes on the character of whatever it dwells upon, and so a mind occupied with good things slowly becomes better suited to receive them. Ordinary experience supports at least part of this, because what we pay attention to day after day shapes our moods, our habits and our choices. The only real question is how far the effect of this habit of mind reaches beyond ourselves and our own moods.

Begin, says Wattles, by giving thanks for what you already possess, however small it may seem, since the person who is not thankful for a little will not be thankful for a great deal. A warm room, a meal, a friendly face or a day of health may all be counted among the gifts. Many people who try this simple exercise say that it changes the way they see an ordinary day.

Those who spend their days complaining about what they lack, Wattles argues, keep their minds fixed on poverty and so remain in its shadow. Their thoughts return again and again to what is missing, and they come to expect more of the same. Psychologists have noticed something similar, since constant complaint tends to make people notice the worst and overlook the rest.

Gratitude, says Wattles, must be a lively and sincere feeling and not merely a polite phrase repeated by habit. Words said without feeling are like a coin without value, and they cannot connect a person to anything. It is a fair point, because a thankful heart is quite different from a thankful speech.

Wattles recommends that his readers spend some of their leisure hours in thankful thought, and a practical way to follow the advice is to keep a small notebook. Each evening one may record three good things from the day, however modest, and read the list again at the next sitting. After a few weeks this simple routine can change what a person notices, which is no small gain.

Gratitude need not stay private, for it can also be spoken aloud to the people who have helped us along the way. A colleague, a teacher, a customer or a friend who hears sincere thanks is more likely to help again, and more likely to feel that the work has been worthwhile. This is a modest and sensible extension of Wattles's idea, and it costs nothing at all.

Researchers who study well-being have found that people who keep a habit of gratitude tend to feel happier and to get on better with others. The habit does not, however, pay the rent, and it would be unkind to tell someone in real hardship that thankfulness alone will solve the problem. Gratitude and the wish to change one's circumstances can live side by side, and the best advice combines the two.

Gratitude, then, is the foundation on which Wattles builds the rest of his method, and everything else in his teaching rests upon it. The second step is to form a clear and definite picture of what you want, which he treats in the eighth chapter. That is the step that many readers remember best, and it is the one that we shall consider next.

Chapter eight is about thinking in the Certain Way, and its first demand is simple and vivid. You must form a clear and definite mental picture of the thing that you want, Wattles says, and keep it before your mind. Many of the best known ideas of the book come from this chapter, and it is where its appeal to the imagination is strongest.

A vague longing, Wattles says, is of very little use, for no one can transmit an idea that he does not himself possess. To ask for something we must first know what it is, and a cloudy wish for more can only produce a cloudy result. Most goal-setting advice today begins in just the same way, by asking a person exactly what he wants.

The mental picture should be exact, Wattles insists, and filled with every detail that can be imagined, from the colour of the door to the view from the window. The reader is to see the thing as though it were already in his hands and to think of it often with pleasure. Whatever its power over the universe, this practice certainly gives the mind something definite to aim at.

Wattles asks his readers to set aside time every day for going over the picture in the mind, until it is fixed there as clearly as a familiar street. Repeating it often and with pleasure, he says, is how the impression is made on the thinking stuff, and so the practice is meant to become a habit. The advice is a kind of rehearsal, and rehearsal is how most human skills are learned, from music to sport to public speaking.

Think of a sailor who keeps one eye on the compass through every storm, and you have an image that fits Wattles's advice about how the picture should be held. Whatever the waves and the wind may do, the ship is steered toward the harbour, and the sailor does not forget the destination for a single hour. Steady attention to a goal is indeed one of the oldest secrets of getting anything done.

Wattles tells his readers to be definite about three things, namely what they want to have, what they want to do and what they want to become. The last two are easy to forget, for many people think only of possessions and neglect the question of what kind of person they hope to be. A balanced picture includes all three of them, and it is the better and the more lasting for it.

For the picture to last, the wish behind it must be real and warm, since a half-hearted idea fades as soon as the day becomes busy. Wattles wants his readers to long for the thing with their whole hearts, and he treats this longing as a source of energy and not as a weakness. Few people ever finish anything difficult without some such fire burning steadily inside them from the start to the finish.

Research on goal setting has generally found that specific goals help people more than vague ones, because they tell the mind exactly what to look for and when it has been reached. This is one of the places where Wattles and modern psychologists agree, though they would explain the reason differently. A clear goal works by guiding our own attention and effort, which is a reason that does not depend on any theory about the universe.

Some researchers have found that dreaming only of the happy ending can quietly drain a person's energy, because the mind enjoys the reward as though it had already been won. Thinking carefully about the steps and the likely obstacles seems to work better than pleasant daydreams alone. A wise reader will therefore keep the vision that Wattles recommends but will add a plan, as he himself does when he turns to action.

Before one fixes a picture firmly in the mind, it is wise to examine it with some honesty. It should show something that the person truly wants, and not what friends, advertisements or rivals have taught him to want, and it should harm nobody else in the getting. A picture that passes these tests is far more likely to keep its power over the years.

A clear picture alone is not enough, Wattles says, and the second half of chapter eight turns to faith. The reader must believe that the thing pictured is already on its way, and must hold that belief steadily through good days and bad. He treats faith as a working part of the method and not as a pleasant extra.

Think of what you want, says Wattles, as something that already belongs to you, since in thought it is already yours. A guest who has been promised a gift behaves with quiet confidence and does not beg or fret, and this is the attitude that Wattles wants his readers to cultivate. Confidence of this kind can be calming, although it must never become an excuse for ignoring facts.

Every doubt, Wattles warns, is a thought of not having the thing that one wants, and it works against the clear picture that one is trying to hold. He therefore advises his readers to put doubt and fear away, and to answer them with calm faith. The advice is easier to give than to follow, since everyone feels doubt now and then, and a sensible person learns to feel it without being ruled by it.

Wattles advises his readers to keep their plans private, unless the listener is someone who believes in them. A careless remark from a sceptical friend can shake a resolve that was built with great care, and sympathy from the right person can strengthen it. There is some wisdom in this, although we should also remember that honest criticism from a trusted friend is sometimes exactly what a plan needs.

Wattles takes the idea of gratitude one step further, and asks the reader to give thanks for what he wants even before it has arrived. The heart is to be thankful as though the gift were already in the room, and this attitude is supposed to keep the faith alive. It is a hard thing to do honestly, and most people will find it easier to be thankful for a sure step forward than for a thing still far away.

Psychologists who study self-belief have found that people who trust in their ability to do a task often keep trying for longer, and so they often do better. This may be the real and ordinary reason why faith seems to help, since persistence is a quality that every success story has in common. It does not require any thinking stuff, only a mind that refuses to give up too soon.

Faith must never take the place of careful thinking, and a person who believes in a plan should still check the numbers and weigh the risks. Many fortunes have been lost by people who trusted too eagerly in their luck and did not look hard at the facts. The wisest course is to hold hope and caution together, as a good captain holds both the wheel and the chart.

Faith also needs patience, for good things, like crops, take time to grow and cannot be hurried by wishing. A farmer who plants a field does not dig up the seeds each morning to see whether they have sprouted, and a person who works toward a goal must learn the same calm. Impatience is one of the commonest reasons why worthwhile efforts are abandoned just before they begin to bear fruit.

The picture and the faith, Wattles says, must be renewed again and again, for a single burst of effort will not do the work. He asks the reader to return to them in every free moment, until the thought has become a settled habit of the mind. Habits that are tied to a fixed time, such as the first minutes after waking, are indeed the ones that are most likely to last.

After the picture and the faith, Wattles turns to the will, which many readers expect to be the engine of success. His answer may surprise them, for he says plainly what the will is for and what it must never be used to do. That answer is the subject of the next two chapters of his book, and it contains some of his most debated advice.

Chapter nine takes up the question of the will, and Wattles begins with a firm prohibition. You must not try to use your will on anything outside yourself, he says, whether that is the universe, other people or the course of events. The will is, in his view, a tool for governing one's own thoughts and actions, and for nothing else.

To try to push the universe around by sheer force of will is a foolish thing, in Wattles's opinion, because the power behind all things is already on your side. The idea that one must wrestle or bargain with it for favours rests on a mistake about its nature. Many people who find his larger theory hard to believe will still agree that endless straining against the world is tiring and often useless.

Nor may the will be used to force other people, Wattles says, for it is wrong to try to make another person do what he would not freely choose. Such an attempt is no better than taking from him by force, and it puts the one who tries on the competitive plane. This is an old moral idea, and it is good to see it stated in a book that might otherwise tempt readers to manipulate.

The proper work of the will, Wattles says, is to govern oneself, to keep one's own thoughts and actions in line with the Certain Way. A person who cannot control his own attention will find it hard to hold a picture or to act with steady purpose. Here the teaching becomes very practical, because self-command is a skill that can be trained.

A traveller reaches the end of a long road by moving his own feet, and by nothing else. He does not try to push the road, or to bend the hills, or to hurry the sun, and he saves his strength for the next step. The will, in the same way, should be spent on the one thing that is truly ours to move.

Self-command means choosing what one will think and do even when one's mood pulls the other way, and it is a skill that grows with practice like any other. A person who gets up at a fixed hour, finishes the hard task first and refuses to brood over every setback is using the will precisely as Wattles describes. The reward is not magic, but it is a real and lasting gain in the control that we have over our own days.

Psychologists who study self-control have found that it is helped more by habits and plans than by sheer effort in the moment. Deciding in advance exactly when and where one will act, for example by saying that one will study at the kitchen table after supper, makes it much more likely that the action will happen. This modern finding fits Wattles's stress on steady daily practice, even though it needs no theory of the thinking stuff.

To respect the free choice of other people is part of the discipline that Wattles asks of his readers, and it fits well with his rule of fair dealing. In business one may describe what one offers, with honesty and enthusiasm, but one may not deceive, frighten or press a customer into a decision. A reputation for treating people this way is among the most valuable things a seller can own.

A tired mind cannot hold a purpose firmly, and anyone who has tried to keep a promise to himself at the end of a long, hungry day knows how true that is. Good sleep, regular meals and short breaks make self-control much easier, and they deserve a place in any serious plan. Wattles himself, in a later chapter, will warn against hurry and strain, and the warning is wise.

Having shown that the will belongs to the self, Wattles goes on to say what it should be used to keep out of the mind. His answer surprises many readers, for he tells them to turn their attention away from poverty and from gloomy talk about it. This is one of the most disputed pieces of advice in the whole book, and it deserves a chapter to itself.

Do not study poverty, says Wattles, and do not spend your days talking about its causes and its cruelties. His claim is that the way to put an end to poverty is to think about riches, and that thinking about misery only keeps it alive. It is a startling piece of advice, and it is the part of his teaching that modern readers most often reject.

The reasoning behind this advice is that the mind is shaped by what it dwells upon, and that the shapes it takes then show up in a person's life. A mind full of poverty, in Wattles's view, will see poverty everywhere, and so will find no way out of it. The idea has some truth, because attention steers our choices, but it is a long step from there to a cure for hunger.

Wattles tells his readers to avoid pessimistic books and articles which claim that the world is going to the bad, since he thinks they fill the mind with the wrong pictures. He wants the attention fixed firmly on whatever is hopeful and whatever is growing, and not on what is decaying. A moderate version of this is wise, for no one is helped by an endless diet of alarming news.

The best service that anyone can do for the poor, Wattles argues, is to become rich in the right spirit and so to show that it can be done. An example of that kind, he says, lifts others by inspiring them, whereas pity leaves them where they were. It is an interesting thought, and it contains some truth, but it is not the whole of what a generous person can do.

Gifts of money may ease a hard day, Wattles agrees, but he believes that they do nothing to end poverty for good. Only the knowledge of how to rise, he says, can do that, and so he puts his faith in teaching and example above charity. Many people today would say that we need both, since a hungry person cannot wait for a lesson while his children are crying.

Most modern readers find this advice far too simple, because poverty has many causes, among them illness, low pay, war, lack of schooling and unfair treatment. Doctors, teachers, charities and governments that look straight at poverty have eased a great deal of real suffering, and they could not have done so by looking away. A fair verdict is that attention to the problem is needed, though attention alone is never enough.

The useful kernel of the advice is that a steady stream of bad news can wear a person down and leave him anxious and tired. Many people find that they feel better and think more clearly when they choose with care what they read and watch each day. Choosing is not the same as hiding, and a thoughtful person can stay informed without living in the middle of every disaster.

Behind his advice lies a cheerful optimism, for Wattles believes that the whole world is moving slowly toward the good. In his view a hopeful outlook is not foolish but sensible, because it matches the direction in which life is actually going. Whether one shares his faith or not, hope is a powerful fuel, and people who have it often accomplish more.

Wattles also advises readers to turn away from gloomy conversation and to seek out people and ideas that give them hope. The company we keep, he believes, shapes the thoughts that we hold, and thoughts in turn shape what we do. Most of us have felt how one cheerful friend can lift a whole evening, and how one grumbler can spoil it.

A person can care deeply about the sufferings of others and still keep a hopeful mind, and the best reformers have usually done both. Wattles's next chapter asks how to keep hope steady against the doubts and distractions of the day, and it develops his idea of purpose. It is a short chapter, but it holds some of his most heartfelt advice.

Chapter ten returns to the use of the will, and it is concerned with faith and with purpose. Wattles says that the wish to get rich must be strong and must last, so that it becomes a steady direction and not a passing mood. Most of us know how many fine resolutions fade within a week, and this chapter is his answer to that common problem.

When the facts around you look discouraging, Wattles says, you should look past them to the picture that you are holding, and refuse to treat the present as final. Appearances, on this view, are only the last chapter of an old story and not the ending of the next one. This is a stirring thought, though it must be balanced by the plain duty to understand what the facts really are.

Some appearances are simply facts, like an unpaid bill or a failing shop, and no amount of hopeful thinking will make them disappear. A wise person faces such facts honestly, makes a plan to deal with them and still keeps the larger aim in view. The courage to do both at once is rarer than either cheerfulness or realism taken alone.

A good driver keeps his eyes on the road ahead, glancing at the scenery only briefly, and Wattles asks the same discipline of the mind. The goal is to be kept in view each day, so that the small events of the hour do not carry the traveller off course. Attention is a limited resource, and those who spend it deliberately generally travel farther.

A wish drifts through the mind like smoke, while a purpose is a decision that stands like a pillar. Wattles wants his readers to turn every wish that matters into a purpose by committing themselves to it and to the steps that it requires. Many people say that they would like to write a book or start a business, but only those who decide, and then act, ever do.

Words are part of the habit of thought, Wattles suggests, and so he urges his readers to speak of themselves and their hopes in hopeful terms. A person who is forever calling himself a failure will find it hard to rise, for the words go on working long after they are spoken. Honest self-criticism is useful, but there is a great difference between saying that I made a mistake and saying that I am nothing.

Thomas Edison and his helpers tested a very large number of materials before they found a thread that would glow in a light bulb for long enough to be useful. Each failed attempt could have been taken as a sign that the task was hopeless, and a weaker purpose would have given up early. The story is often told to show that persistence matters, and there is no reason to doubt that it does.

Wattles wants the purpose to fit within a larger good, so that a person's aim adds to life, including the lives of other people, and does not subtract from them. A purpose that serves only vanity or spite is likely to be weak and short-lived, while one that serves a family or a community can sustain a person through years of work. Most people find their deepest strength when what they do matters to someone else.

A steady purpose is not sustained by thought alone, for the mind that holds it needs rest, healthy food and the company of good friends. Constant stress can wear down even the strongest resolve, as anyone who has worked too hard for too long will know. Taking care of the body is therefore part of taking care of the purpose, and Wattles's plain advice about calm and steadiness points in the same direction.

Wattles has now explained how to hold the picture, the faith and the purpose, and he is ready to turn from thought to deed. His next chapter says firmly that all this thinking is useless unless it is joined to action, and he calls the failure to join them the rock on which many otherwise sensible thinkers are wrecked. It is the part of the book that no one needs to doubt, and it is the part that every reader can use.

In chapter eleven Wattles says that thought is the creative power, or at least the force that sets it moving, but that thought alone will not bring riches. Many logical thinkers are wrecked on one rock, he says, which is the failure to connect their thought with personal action. It is one of the most useful warnings in the book, and it is the point at which his philosophy joins common sense.

Thought, in Wattles's scheme, is the guide and action is the vehicle, and the two must travel together. The things that a person wants come through the work that he does, and not through the pictures that he merely holds. Anyone who has tried to learn a language or to build a business by wishing alone will recognise the truth of that.

You can act only in the present, Wattles reminds us, for the past is over and the future has not yet arrived. Time spent in regret about yesterday, or in speculation about tomorrow, is time that cannot be used for the one thing that makes a difference. The thought is as old as many philosophies, and it is a remarkably practical one for anyone inclined to procrastinate.

Act where you are, says Wattles, and not in the place where you used to be or in the place where you would like to be. You cannot act in a spot that you have not yet reached, and so a person who waits for better surroundings will wait for a very long time. Better surroundings are usually the consequence of good work done in the present ones, which is a hopeful fact indeed.

Do not wait for a change of environment, Wattles says, for it is by acting upon the present one that a better one is created. The clerk who masters his small desk, the worker who improves his own corner of the factory and the farmer who tends his own poor field are all making the next step possible. It is a patient doctrine, but it has the merit of being something that anyone can begin this morning.

Do not wait for a great opportunity to appear, Wattles says, but do what you can today with the tools and the knowledge that you already possess. Small acts done well prepare the way for larger ones, and the habit of starting is more valuable than any perfect plan that is never begun. Many successful people in every field have told much the same story about their beginnings.

Imagine a young clerk with no savings who takes the trouble to learn every part of the shop where he works, from the stockroom to the accounts. Without spending a single coin he is preparing himself for a better position, and when a vacancy occurs he will be the obvious choice. This is the kind of quiet progress that Wattles has in mind when he says to act where one is.

A person who feels that he is in the wrong kind of work, Wattles says, should not wait until he is in the right one before he begins to act. He should do the present work as well as it can be done, and treat it as a step toward something better. Employers and customers notice such workers, and they have a way of finding the doors that lead onward.

Thought without action, however vivid, is only daydreaming, and a plan without a first step remains no more than a wish. Wattles knows this, which is why he follows his chapters on the picture with chapters on work, and why he insists that the two belong together. A reader who takes only the dreaming from his book and leaves the doing has misunderstood him.

A modern reader will add that acting now does not mean acting rashly, and that the sensible path is to start small, test the idea and learn from the result. Risking only what one can afford to lose keeps a bad beginning from becoming a disaster, and it leaves room for a second try. Wattles himself would agree, for his next chapter is all about doing each act with care.

Chapter twelve is about efficient action, and it makes two clear demands upon the reader. You must do each day all that can be done that day, Wattles says, and you must do each separate act in an efficient manner. The first demand is about quantity and the second about quality, and a careful reader will notice that he cares more for the second.

Make every act a success in itself, Wattles says, for the whole of a life is built from separate acts, one after another. If each of them is done well, the sum can hardly be a failure, and if each is done poorly, no amount of faith will rescue the total. It is a reassuring thought for anyone who feels overwhelmed, because it turns a huge ambition into a series of small and finishable tasks.

A careless act is a loss, Wattles says, and the time and the chance that it wastes cannot be made up later by any amount of regret. For that reason he asks his readers never to put half of their effort into anything, even a task that seems trivial. Employers have always valued the person who takes the same trouble over a small job as over a large one.

Do not try to do tomorrow's work today, nor a whole week's work in a single day, Wattles warns, for it is not the number of things that you do which matters. What counts is the efficiency of each separate action, and one thing done thoroughly is worth more than ten things done in a rush. The counsel will be familiar to anyone who has tried to do too many things at once and ended up doing none of them well.

Do not hurry and do not worry, Wattles says, for hurry and worry are the enemies of good work. A calm mind and a steady pace carry a person much further than a headlong rush, and a person who is afraid cannot think clearly or act well. Here modern advice about stress and about slow, steady effort agrees closely with his own.

While you work, Wattles says, keep the vision in the back of your mind, so that every task you perform becomes a step toward the goal and not merely a way of passing time. This is the difference between a person who is simply busy and one who is going somewhere. Even a dull task becomes easier to bear when we can see how it fits into something that we care about.

Success is rarely one dramatic event, and it is far more often the quiet result of small habits that are repeated every day. A person who does a little well each day will, over the course of a year, have accomplished a great deal, and over ten years a very great deal indeed. Wattles's stress on daily action points exactly in this direction, and on this point nearly everyone would agree with him.

Research on how people learn skills has found that they grow through steady practice, especially when the learner gets honest feedback and corrects mistakes. Wattles's call for efficient action in each task fits this finding well, because efficiency comes with repetition and with attention to what works. The best performers in music, sport and trade are rarely those who rest on talent, and far more often those who practise with care.

A simple habit can make the teaching of this chapter real, and it takes only a few minutes at the end of each day. Look back over the hours that have passed, ask honestly which acts were done well and which were done carelessly, and decide how to improve tomorrow's. A person who does this for a year will probably find that the improvement is large and that it was bought quite cheaply.

Rest matters as much as effort, because a rested worker does better work than an exhausted one and makes fewer costly mistakes. Studies have repeatedly linked long periods of poor sleep with worse judgment, worse mood and worse health, and so overwork can defeat its own purpose. Wattles's call to do all that can be done in a day should therefore be read as a call to do it well, and not as a call to do it until we drop.

Chapter thirteen is about getting into the right business, and Wattles begins with a plain observation. Each kind of work, he says, needs its own kind of talent, so that a music teacher needs musical ability and a mechanic needs mechanical skill. It is hard to argue with this, and it leads naturally to the question of how a person finds the work that suits him.

Having the talent for a trade is not enough to get rich, Wattles warns, and he points to the skilled musicians, blacksmiths and carpenters who remain poor all their lives. What they lack, he says, is not ability but the Certain Way of thinking and acting, and with it they could prosper in the same work. Modern readers will add that markets, location and luck also affect what a skill is paid.

A person may have talent for many different kinds of work, Wattles says, and the best choice among them is the work that he most wishes to do. Desire is a guide that points to where the energy will flow most freely, and an occupation that one longs for will be pursued with more patience. Choosing in this way does not guarantee success, but it makes the long labour much easier to bear.

The desire to do a particular thing, Wattles says, is a sign that the power to do it is already present and is asking for a way to be used. A child who longs to play music, he suggests, has within her the beginnings of a musician. A modern reader would add that interest often does grow into skill, but that wanting alone is never ability, and that long practice must come between the two.

A lack of training need not stop a person from reaching toward the work that he loves, since many skills can be learned with time, effort and good teachers. Night classes, apprenticeships and borrowed books have served countless people who began with no advantage but their determination. The path may be slower than it would be for those who start with schooling, but it is open.

Do not be afraid of choosing wrongly, Wattles says, for a person who has made a mistake in his choice of work can always change course. The work he does in the meantime is not wasted if it is done well, because it teaches him what he does and does not want. Many people have found their true calling only after two or three false starts, and the lessons of the early attempts often proved useful.

A practical way to choose one's work is to ask three questions and to answer them with honesty. What do I enjoy, what am I able to do well, and what do other people need or want enough to pay for? Work that sits where the three answers overlap tends to be the most satisfying, and it is also the work that Wattles's rule of use value would favour.

The kind of work that one hopes for should be part of the picture that one holds in the mind, Wattles says, so that the vision includes what one wishes to do as well as what one wishes to own. This links the thirteenth chapter back to the eighth, and shows how the parts of his plan fit together. A goal with a calling inside it is far more likely to last than one that is only about possessions.

It must be said that not everyone is free to choose their work, because bills, family duties and the jobs that exist in one's own town all limit the possibilities. Wattles's encouraging words are most easily taken by those who have some room to move, and they may sound hollow to someone with no room at all. A fair reading is that choice is a matter of degree, and that even a small step toward better-suited work is worth taking.

A sensible plan is to keep a steady income while one tries something new, so that a bad start does not become a crisis. It also helps to talk with people who already work in the field, since they can describe the hours, the pay and the difficulties that no book will tell you. After that, the next chapter of Wattles's book asks how to deal with others in whatever work one has chosen.

Chapter fourteen is about what Wattles calls the impression of increase, and its advice applies whether a person stays in his present trade or enters a new one. In either case, he says, you must give every person you meet the feeling that dealing with you adds to their lives. The chapter is, in effect, a lesson in what we would now call good service.

Each customer should leave with the feeling that he has received more than he paid for, Wattles says, and so the seller must give real value that the buyer can feel. This feeling cannot be faked by clever talk for long, because a customer soon discovers whether the goods and the service are good. It is the same rule of use value and cash value that we met earlier, now applied to the whole manner of doing business.

The sense of increase, in Wattles's opinion, does not come from tricks but from the giver's own faith and purpose, which people are able to feel. A seller who truly believes that his goods will do good, and who is on the way toward something he cares about, carries that conviction in his manner. Most customers trust a person who seems sure and honest far more than one who seems anxious to get the sale.

The impression should be carried, Wattles says, into every part of a person's work, so that it can be felt in his words, in his letters, in his manner and in the way that he finishes each task. A neat reply, a promise kept and a friendly greeting may seem small, but together they create a reputation that no advertisement can buy. Every successful business has been built on such small things done reliably, again and again.

People are drawn, Wattles says, to the person who gives them a sense of gain, and trade will come to him as a stream comes to the sea. Customers who feel well treated come back, and they tell their friends, so that the reputation of a good business grows by itself. This part of his teaching is in line with ordinary experience, because word of mouth has always been among the best forms of advertising.

The same rule applies in the professions, Wattles says, and he names the teacher, the doctor and the minister as people who should add to the life of everyone they serve. A teacher who leaves pupils feeling that they have grown, or a doctor who leaves patients feeling that their lives are in better hands, has given them increase of the best kind. Such work is its own reward, even though it does not always make the worker rich.

Think of a teacher whose pupils leave each lesson feeling that they have grown in skill, in knowledge and in confidence, and who remember that feeling for the rest of their lives. That is the kind of increase that Wattles has in mind, and it is something that money measures poorly. The same is true of the nurse, the builder and the cook, whose work adds something to the life of those who receive it.

The increase must be real, and Wattles would have no sympathy with a seller who tried to create the impression with false claims or loud promises. A seller who deceives a customer may make a profit for a day, but he loses the one thing that a business can never buy back, which is trust. The cure, Wattles would say, is to give actual use value and to let the feeling of increase arise from that.

Good service is a sound foundation for any business, but it does not guarantee success, and a modern reader will want to say so plainly. Price, location, timing, competition and plain luck all matter as well, and many kind and honest businesses have closed their doors. Wattles's chapter is best read as a description of what to aim for and not as a promise of what the market will pay.

So far Wattles has spoken mainly to people who run their own shops and businesses, or who work for themselves in a profession. In the next chapter he turns to the employee, who may feel that his advice is meant for somebody else, and he insists that it is meant for him too. The employee's route to growth, in his account, is a steady one, and it begins with the work already in hand.

Chapter fifteen is written for people who work for others, and Wattles tells them that they need not stay in their present place. The employee who wishes to rise he calls the Advancing Man, and he describes this person as someone who grows by steady effort and not by waiting for a lucky break. It is an encouraging chapter, and much of its advice is sensible whatever one thinks of the rest.

The Advancing Man, says Wattles, does every day a little more than he is paid for, giving more in use value than he takes in wages. This is the rule of the whole book applied to the humble position of the employee, and it is meant as a way of growth and not as a form of servitude. The idea is old, but it still works wherever people notice who is genuinely helpful.

An employer will not want to lose a worker who grows steadily more useful, Wattles says, and if this one will not reward him, another will. He believes that real usefulness cannot be hidden for long, because someone is always in need of people who can do more than they are asked. This is often true, although reality can be slower and less fair than his words suggest.

Prepare for the next position before you have it, Wattles says, and learn the skills of the next level of work while you are still doing the present one. A young clerk who studies bookkeeping in the evenings, or a young mechanic who learns to read plans, will be ready when the vacancy occurs. Preparation of this kind is slow and quiet, but it makes luck far more likely to find a person at home.

The Advancing Man does not sit and wait for luck or for favours from others, Wattles says, for he knows what he is working toward. Each day he does his work with the picture in mind, so that every task is a step on a road that he has chosen. Waiting for luck is a poor plan, and Wattles is right that active preparation gives chance something to work with.

The work of the Advancing Man, Wattles says, should come from faith and purpose and not from the fear of being dismissed. Fear makes a person smaller and clumsier, and it fills the mind with pictures of loss in place of pictures of growth. It is easier to give this advice than to take it when the rent is due, but the principle holds that calm people usually work better.

A modern reader will want to add that extra effort should be paired with honest asking, since managers cannot always guess what an employee hopes for. A worker can request training, volunteer for new tasks, keep a record of her achievements and ask for fair pay when the work has grown. Quiet excellence is admirable, but it is far more effective when the right people also know about it.

It must also be admitted that some employers do not reward extra effort, and that doing more for nothing, year after year, can be simply unfair. A wise worker therefore watches whether the extra work is leading anywhere, and she is ready to look elsewhere if it is not. Wattles's own spirit would allow this, since the whole book teaches that no one is chained to a place that offers no growth.

When a place offers no more room to grow, the Advancing Man may move on, and Wattles wants him to do so calmly and without bitterness. He leaves with the good name that he has earned, and with the skills that he has built, which he carries into whatever comes next. A person who departs in this manner often finds that old colleagues are glad to help him later.

Step by step, and one day at a time, an employee can rise, and Wattles holds that there is no ceiling above the person who keeps growing. He now turns to his closing chapters, which gather together a few cautions and a summary of the whole method. We shall follow him there, and then make up our own minds about what to keep.

In chapter sixteen Wattles expects that some readers will sneer at the very idea of a science of getting rich, and he offers a simple reply. Try the method, he says, and judge it by what happens, and do not be put off by what the doubters say. The invitation is fair as far as it goes, but results have to be measured honestly, and that is harder than it sounds.

If a person fails, Wattles says, the fault must lie in the doing and not in the method, which means that he did not follow the Certain Way fully. A modern reader will see the difficulty at once, for a claim which can never be proved wrong, whatever happens, cannot really be tested at all. This is the most serious weakness of the book, and it is a good reason to take its promises with a grain of salt.

Wattles recommends that the reader keep the book close, read it every day and, if possible, commit it to memory. He adds that one should not busy oneself with rival systems of thought until the method has been fully tried, since conflicting ideas may breed doubt. A habit of rereading is useful, but a thoughtful person will go on reading widely, and will never let any single book forbid the others.

Chapter seventeen is a summary of the whole method, set out as a list of short statements. It begins with the thinking stuff from which all things are made, and with the claim that a thought held in it brings forth the thing imagined. It then says that a person must pass from the competitive mind to the creative one, since the great intelligence behind the world is creative and never competitive.

The summary then repeats the two practices that Wattles loves best, namely deep gratitude and the clear and definite mental picture. The person who wishes to get rich should spend his leisure hours in contemplating the vision and in thanksgiving that it is being given, he says, and should do so with a faith that does not waver. These are the habits that many readers remember when they have forgotten the rest of the book.

Next the summary reminds the reader that the creative power works through the established channels of natural growth and of the industrial and social order. For that reason a person must be in action, doing every day all that can be done that day, and doing each act in an efficient manner. Here, once more, the practical heart of the book shows through, and it is the part that most readers will find easiest to use.

The summary closes with the rule of giving more in use value than one takes in cash value, and with the impression of increase. Wattles then makes his boldest promise, that those who do this will get rich in exact proportion to the definiteness of their vision, the fixity of their purpose, the steadiness of their faith and the depth of their gratitude. No book can truly keep such a promise, but it shows how strongly he believed in his message.

Much of what Wattles recommends stands up well to the test of ordinary experience. Clear goals, a thankful heart, steady daily work, honest service to others, and a hopeful and unhurried mind are all habits that most people would be glad to have, and none of them requires a belief in any thinking stuff. Taken in that spirit, his book is a useful reminder of things that we already half know.

Other claims do not stand up so well, for there is no evidence that thoughts alone can create objects, and the promise of certain riches cannot be tested. The advice to look away from poverty and from hard facts can also do real harm, because problems that are ignored seldom go away. A sensible reader will therefore make plans, test ideas in small steps, seek advice from people who know the field, and take care of health, family and honesty along the way.

Wattles died in 1911, only a year after his book appeared, and yet more than a century later it is still read around the world by people who hope for a better life. It is best taken as a philosophy of effort and attitude, a mixture of useful habits and large beliefs that cannot be proved. Read it with an open mind, test its ideas against your own experience, and keep what proves true.
